#3511. 10 Hacks Every Reddit User Should Know

If you're looking for discussions, recommendations, or advice online, it's hard to avoid Reddit. From mainstream sports to niche crafts, it does seem that there's some kind of Reddit community for everyone. (And if there's not one, you can make one yourself.) If you're using Reddit, here are 10 hacks you should know about to improve your experience on the site.

Reddit used to let everyone view your post and comment history, but in recent years, you can make your profile private. You can hide your posts, comments, and the subreddits you're a part of. If you want to do this, click your profile icon once you've logged in to Reddit, and go to Settings > Profile. Alternatively, you can follow the direct link to Reddit's profile settings page. Click the drop-down menu next to Content & Activity, and select Hide all. You should also turn off Online Status on the same page to stop people from seeing when you're using Reddit.

Old Reddit lets you use the site's classic design, and I prefer it to the more modern UI. Old Reddit looks dated, but it doesn't have infinite scrolling, distracting animations, and a bunch of features designed to increase the time you spend on the platform. It's no wonder that Reddit is making it harder to access this version of the site. As long as it's around, you should switch to Old Reddit for a cleaner reading experience. You can do that by going to Reddit Settings > Preferences and enabling Default to Old Reddit. You can also visit old.reddit.com, though you'll need to sign in for access

Many subreddits use custom themes that range from beautiful to borderline unusable. If you want a more consistent UI across the site, you should disable these custom subreddit styles. Go to Reddit Settings > Preferences and turn off Use community themes. If you're using Old Reddit, click the preferences button in the top-right corner, and under "display options," disable allow subreddits to show me custom themes.

A multireddit is a feed that shows posts from a customized group of subreddits. You can think of it as a way to break out of Reddit's algorithms, and create your own Reddit feed. I use multireddits to follow all sports-related subs I'm interested in. I even have one for gaming, and one for fountain pens. It's a great way to create interest-specific feeds, and if you make them private, no one else can see them. To create one, click the Create custom feed button in the left pane in new Reddit. In the Old Reddit design, click the Create button in the left pane. Be sure to select the Private button to keep it from showing up for others. You can add as many subreddits as you like to the list, and bookmark the feed to access it whenever you wish to.

Reddit has recently adopted an Instagram-like experience for its feeds. It removed the ability to sort posts by new, controversial, best, etc., and instead offers "For You" and "Following." If you dislike this change, you can bypass it. I use Reddit on mobile Safari, and I recommend an extension called Sink It for Reddit. It can automatically redirect you to Old Reddit, and there's a feature that optimizes it for mobile, which brings back the old sorting options. You can also use third-party apps such as RedReader for Android, or RDX for Reddit on an iPhone or iPad to restore the old sorting options for Reddit posts.

After all these years, Reddit's built-in search still leaves something to be desired—at least, on the surface. To find posts on Reddit faster, use search filters on the site. For instance, adding "title:" to your search will limit the results to post titles, and boolean operators such as AND, OR, and NOT also work for advanced searches on the site.

#3510. Dolly Parton on Her Mother Avie Lee Parton’s Album, Mama Sings

Many people know of my mama, Avie Lee Owens Parton, from my song “Coat of Many Colors,” but my mama gave me a gift that was far more valuable than a colorful coat. She gave me the gift of music.

As far back as I can remember, Mama loved to sing—at church, at family get-togethers, and most of all to her children. Her love of music came naturally; she had inherited it from her parents, her grandparents, and all the way back to Wales, where her family, the Owens, came from. Most of all, she inherited her love of music from her father, the Rev. Jake Owens. Grandpa Owens was a singer, songwriter, musician, and music teacher, in addition to being a full time Pentecostal preacher. He and my grandma Rena raised eight children, and all of them took to music in one way or another.

So, it was a natural thing that Mama shared her love of music with her children. She especially loved the old mountain songs—ballads that reached all the way back to the British Isles, popular songs from the 1800s that mountain people had made their own and, of course, beloved hymns.

So, when my uncle Louis Owens, Porter Wagoner, and I opened Fireside Recording Studio in Nashville in 1973, both my uncle Louis and I knew we had to get Mama in the recording studio to capture her songs on tape. Working with just a guitarist and an autoharp player, Mama recorded her own versions of some of her favorite songs.

Dolly Parton, Carl Butler, Avie Lee Parton, Robert Lee Parton, and Pearl Butler.

The plan was to release an album, but for one reason or another, it never happened. Fortunately, my uncle Louis saved all the tapes, and when he passed away, his son Richie, who has always loved our family history and heritage, decided to clean them up and get them released.

Dolly Parton and her mother, Avie Lee Parton.

Many of them are well-known tunes, but you may know them under different titles. Like all mountain singers, Mama preferred to call songs by the name she’d learned them under, and we decided that that was the way we needed to present them to you.

If you’ve ever wondered where my music came from, this album tells the story, and I am so proud, happy, and honored to have shared this music and my mama’s voice with you.

What's it like to hang out with Cliff Booth without Rick Dalton?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I had the chance to see The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth at its glitzy Los Angeles premiere earlier this week, and I must say, I think fans of Once Upon A Time… In Hollywood are in for a treat. The sequel comes from an original script by Quentin Tarantino, and stars Brad Pitt under the direction of Se7en and Fight Club’s David Fincher. Talk about a dream trio! The reviews just dropped for the 1977-set flick, and a lot of people are bringing up something that could have been that I thought about myself.

Word on the street is that when Quentin Tarantino first wrote the script for the Cliff Booth movie, it was reportedly a sprawling 230 pages. This prompted Pitt and Fincher, the latter being exclusive to Netflix, to have discussions about whether it should be a movie or TV series. They ended up making it one of the latest 2026 movie releases, but as many reviews point out, there’s a clear feeling it could have been great as an episodic affair. As Variety’s Owen Gleiberman writes:

It’s the first Tarantino film that feels, in its structural DNA, like a glorified television series. At one point, the movie was supposed to be a series, and in spirit that’s kind of what it still is. Call it QT TV. The incidents hook you, but with less consequence than they’d have in a full-blown, let-it-rip Tarantino movie. The Further Mis-Adventures looks like a movie (Fincher gives it a stately sheen), and it’s way too violent for television. But the hangout factor, in this case, feels one small step removed from the characters-on-a-TV-series-are-your-family factor.

One massive pro of it being a movie is that film buffs can experience the crime-comedy on IMAX screens next week, ahead of it being available to stream with a Netflix subscription in December. I very much enjoyed watching it in theaters, especially for all the audience reactions. I should also point out the film very much has the three-act structure of a movie, and doesn’t feel unfinished. However, it definitely feels like there’s a bigger world Tarantino has created that the film didn't have time to fully get to. Check out what The Hollywood Reporter’s David Rooney said on the subject:

Often, The Further Mis-Adventures is so busy swooning over Brad/Cliff that it plays like episodic TV or part of a pulpy paperback series built around the lovable reprobate character. It’s less robust as a feature-length narrative, though that doesn’t make it any less entertaining. Tarantino disciples will eat it up, while Fincher obsessives should find plenty of the director’s pungent atmospherics, his technical flair and moody visual style.

Cliff Booth has an incredible cast that features some especially memorable parts for Elizabeth Debicki, as a talent agent and the object of Cliff’s affections, and Scott Caan, who plays a popular TV star who needs Cliff’s particular set of skills. But then there are characters like Yahya Abdul-Mateen II’s Roderick "Hot Rod" Harrison and Carla Gugino’s Toni Peters, who feel less meaty than they could have been. Here’s what IndieWire’s David Ehrich said about the movie, which he also called a “disappointing compromise between great directors”:

Tarantino might be drawn to the discursive plotting of an Elmore Leonard paperback, but after watching any number of Netflix TV shows that should have been shortened into movies, it’s a cruel irony to see two of our greatest filmmakers slush their talents together into a movie that should have serialized into a long-running TV show, complete with a new guest star every week.

Outside of the conversation around how making Cliff Booth into a movie might have been a missed opportunity, there’s a lot of glowing praise for the film. Screen Daily’s Tim Grierson was particularly impressed by the mashup between filmmakers, writing:

With Cliff Booth, Fincher honours Tarantino’s maximalist aesthetic and colourful idiosyncrasies, although in the script’s shockingly brutal action sequences he applies the steely style that has been the hallmark of his own gripping thrillers. Nonetheless, by allowing Tarantino’s amusingly meandering dialogue to flourish, the director has created a warmer, more relaxed picture than is typical from this master of brooding tone.

Then there’s a four-star review from The Guardian’s Peter Bradshaw. The critic called Pitt’s performance “endlessly watchable and entertaining, but also enigmatic,” along with noting these thoughts about the filmmaking:

Fincher’s direction perhaps speeds things up in the scene transitions, quicker than the chapter-by-chapter prolixity that Tarantino would have favoured. Female characters also tend to keep their shoes and socks on.

Overall, the reviews are skewing positive, with a few leaning more lukewarm. We saw it coming after all the great first reactions right out of the premiere. Here’s one more thought from Nicolas Barber’s review for the BBC:

More than anything, the film is a loving tribute to the parts of 1970s LA where Tinseltown glamour met criminal seediness. Fincher and Tarantino luxuriate in the details of vintage sportscars, landline phones and historic cinemas (which is ironic for a production financed by a streaming service, Netflix). Their gorgeously designed nostalgia-fest is always easy to watch, and it's never boring, but some of its attitudes seem to come from the 1970s, too.

If you loved Once Upon a Time...In Hollywood, I definitely think you should catch this one. I thought the runtime flew by and it was simply a fun time, but all these reactions help gather a broader picture of what people think about it so far.

You can try to catch The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth in theaters on November 25 or wait for the flick to arrive on Netflix on December 23.

#3508. 10 Hacks Every Hulu User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you don't like the content Hulu is suggesting for you, you have several options to curate your recommendations. "Disliking" a show or movie removes it from your Home view and You May Also Like entirely, so the only way you'll see that content is if you search for it. You can dislike on the Details page if you're watching on your TV or use the thumbs down on mobile or web. (The "Like" button will obviously influence your algorithm in the opposite way). If your "Continue Watching" queue is cluttered with shows you started but didn't like enough to finish, you can remove them from your watch history as well as the My Stuff list. This, too, will allow content to remain searchable but not suggested in other areas of the app.

If PIN protection is enabled, users must enter a four-digit PIN when switching between profiles on a single account. This is intended as a parental control feature, since it's available on non-Kids profiles and can keep children from accessing more mature content on an adult's profile. However, you can also enable this feature to keep other users from seeing your viewing history and preferences or influencing your algorithm by watching their content under your profile (accidentally or on purpose). To set up a PIN, log into your account on Hulu's website, select your profile, and go to Manage Profiles > Parental Controls. You'll have to choose a PIN and enter your password to confirm the changes.

Another approach to protecting your profile and algorithm is to set up separate profiles for specific use cases, such as when you have guests or if you host watch parties for certain shows. This keeps content from influencing your recommendations and prevents other viewers from seeing what's in your watch history or saved content (especially if there are things you want to keep private).

If you find that subtitles and captions are too bold—or not visible enough—you can change the font, color, size, and style from the default so they enhance your viewing experience rather than detracting from it. Hulu allows you to adjust the color and opacity of the font, background, and window so you get the right contrast, and you can also select the specific font and font scaling. On your streaming device, go to Settings > Subtitles & Captions, then hit the back button on your remote to save your preferences. You can update these settings on mobile and desktop as well.

If you have a long list of shows and films to watch but can't decide what to start next, look for the "Expiring Soon" badge to see which titles are leaving the service in the next two weeks. Badges display the number of days remaining, so you can determine what to prioritize and whether it's worth diving in based on how much time you have to finish before the expiration date. Go to "My Stuff" to monitor saved titles that are expiring soon.

If you've been watching Hulu under an account shared with family or friends and need to switch to your own subscription, you can transfer your profile to keep your watch history and settings intact instead of starting from scratch. You can initiate a profile transfer on a TV-connected device. Note that account holders have to approve transfer requests within seven days, and once expired, transfer requests cannot be resubmitted—so be sure to let the primary user know that you've made the request.

If you've shared your Hulu login information with friends or activated your account on devices you don't own, you may want to regularly audit where your account is being used and remove any that don't need access. This includes TVs in Airbnbs and hotels. If you stay logged in, unauthorized users may have access to your Hulu account and personal data. You can see activated devices (and their activation date) under Your Account > Watch Hulu on Your Devices > Manage Devices. Click Remove next to old or unrecognized devices.

Hulu has an offline mode that allows you to download shows and movies to watch when you don't have a network connection. This is useful for traveling or when you know your wifi or cell service will be limited. Downloads are only available on supported iOS and Android devices, which means you may have to consider how much space your content takes up. You can select High for video quality if you want maximum resolution, but you may want to choose Standard if you are short on storage. This option is available under Downloads > Settings > Video Quality on iOS and Account > Settings > Downloads > Video Quality on Android. Note that once you click play on downloaded content, you have 48 hours to watch it before it expires—so don't start it unless you are ready.

If you have a Hulu + Live TV subscription, you must designate a "Home" network, which determines the local channels included in your plan. You can update your location up to four times within a 12-month period, but this limitation is meant to prevent viewers outside a household from sharing a subscription. Hulu does allow you to stream live TV on mobile when you're away from your home network (within the U.S.) as long as you access your account on that network every 30 days. If you travel often, check in with your mobile device frequently to avoid being locked out when you're away. Note that you can still watch streaming content with no restrictions.

#3507. 10 Years Ago Today: Hailee Steinfeld Starred In One Of The Best Coming-Of-Age Movies Of All Time

Actor Hailee Steinfeld broke out in the Coen Brothers' 2010 Western film "True Grit" as the precocious Mattie Ross, who speaks like she's wise beyond her years but lacks the experience that brings true wisdom. We at /Film consider Steinfeld as Mattie the greatest performance in any Coens movie, which is no small feat.

Nominated for an Academy Award at only 14 years old, it would've been easy for Steinfeld's career to have peaked there. But she has kept challenging herself with music, voice acting, and plenty of new movies, and one of her best is absolutely writer/director Kelly Fremon Craig's coming-of-age film "The Edge of Seventeen."

After a premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival, "The Edge of Seventeen" hit theaters on November 18, 2016. It takes its title from the Stevie Nicks song yet applies it more literally to this story about a 17-year-old girl. The acerbic, awkward, and unpopular Nadine Franklin (Steinfeld) has lost the two people in the world who understand her. One, her father, Tom (Eric Keenleyside), who died a few years prior of a heart attack. Now, her best friend, Krista (Haley Lu Richardson), has started dating Nadine's older brother Darian (Blake Jenner), whom Nadine loathes for having their mother Mona's (Kyra Sedgewick) favor and being so effortlessly beloved and successful.

"I've gotta spend the rest of my life with myself," Nadine says while drunk. We all realize that and then come to terms with it at some point. Nadine's story fits in the gap between the realization and the coming to terms. Speaking as someone who was the same age as Nadine was in 2016, and saw "The Edge of Seventeen" in his senior year of high school, few coming-of-age movies depict awkward adolescence in the 2010s more honestly.

Critics compared "The Edge of Seventeen" to a modern John Hughes movie, as did Hailee Steinfeld herself. In 2016, she explained to Entertainment Weekly that she hoped that the movie could reflect her generation's teen years back at them while still being timeless, in the same way "Sixteen Candles" and "The Breakfast Club" — films made for 1980s kids — still resonated with her (someone born in 1996).

But "The Edge of Seventeen" doesn't soften itself by looking to echoes of older movies instead of real life. The film begins with Nadine marching up to her history teacher, Mr. Bruner (Woody Harrelson) in his classroom, announcing she's planning to die by suicide and wants someone to know first. That opening makes you think you're in for a movie about an inspirational teacher who talks a depressed student back from the edge and shows them why life is worth living. Well, not quite.

We see, as Mr. Bruner immediately recognizes, this is Nadine being dramatic. "I don't want to take up a ton of your time" she says right off, which is her first lie. The movie then rewinds (with the help of some voiceover from Nadine, though that fades pretty quickly) before catching back up with this cold open. What led to her current situation? Nadine accidentally sent a text to her crush, Nick (Alexander Calvert), describing very explicitly how she wants to hook up with him.

That complements one of the best bits of writing in the film, one that definitely helped it speak to my younger self. Nadine has a lot of movie-typical teenage boy qualities: she doesn't fit in, dresses in baggy sweatshirts, has a hopeless crush she never talks to, makes sex jokes while mistaking vulgarity for wit, etc.

During the "Edge of Seventeen" press tour, Kelly Fremon Craig and producer James L. Brooks spoke with /Film. Craig cited some "life-altering" writing advice from Brooks, that she needed to ask herself, "What is this movie saying about life?" I would answer that "The Edge of Seventeen" is about how, when you're a teenager, your problems seem like the whole world and that part of growing up is realizing others — even people who irritate you everyday (as Nadine's mom and brother do to her) — are dealing with their own pain.

Upon its release, "The Edge of Seventeen" saw only modest financial success, grossing $19 million in theaters against its $9 million budget. A spin-off TV series ordered by YouTube Red ultimately didn't move forward, either. I would also argue the film's anticipated reputation as "definitive teen movie of the 2010s" was overshadowed by Greta Gerwig's "Lady Bird," which came out the following year and hits similar beats while finding both great financial success and critical acclaim. Not that "The Edge of Seventeen" has been lost to time or anything, though.

In that aforementioned /Film interview, Craig claimed, "If [Hailee Steinfeld] didn't exist, the movie wouldn't exist," because she brought a sui generis quality to Nadine as she once did to Mattie Ross. The two would work together again on the "Transformers" spin-off film "Bumblebee," where Steinfeld starred and Craig performed rewrites. "Bumblebee" often feels like "The Edge of Seventeen" but with Transformers included.

A couple of times in "The Edge of Seventeen," Nadine looks up to the sky and asks if God is even paying attention to her. Perhaps it's not surprising that when Craig directed another coming-of-age film, she adapted Judy Blume's classic novel "Are You There God? It's Me, Margaret."

#3506. How to Make Sure an 'Onion' Site on the Dark Web Is Legitimate

Thankfully, Tor Browser already has a cryptography-backed feature that can verify the authenticity of an onion site, by confirming whether it has end-to-end encryption and extended validation certificates. Here's how this feature works, where it falters, as well as what other red flags you should look for.

While phishing on the dark web works as it does on the clear web, scammers have a few unique advantages due to the secretive nature of the environment. Most importantly, you can’t just glance at an onion link to tell if the site is genuine. Normal website URLs tend to be short and memorable, while onion links are 56-character strings of alphanumeric text that look mostly like gibberish.

When you try to connect, Tor Browser verifies the URL against the originating website’s cryptographic key, which is how you know nobody has hijacked the address or tampered with it midway. But since this has the unwanted effect of making domains harder to recall, scammers have a much easier time generating lookalike addresses or creating website clones.

For example, many popular websites use “vanity prefixes” to make their onion addresses more easily identifiable or to add some branding appeal. That means their 56-character onion link starts with something like “facebook,” “bbcnews,” or “ciadotgov.” But scammers can use a free tool like mkp224o to generate lookalike addresses with the same vanity prefix as the legitimate website, which gives users a false sense of security.

Of course, most dark web users don’t type addresses directly into Tor Browser; they use dark web directories like the Hidden Wiki to find useful onion sites relevant to their search. Scammers will create fake search engines or link directories to point users to their fake websites, like when the Ahmia search engine discovered that a copy of its platform was directing users to 255 cloned services back in 2015.

Of course, it’s possible to orchestrate phishing attempts that don’t involve cloning sites at all. Researchers at Freie Universität Berlin describe a sophisticated technique where attackers serve the real website through their own reverse proxy, which lets them manipulate parts of the site or log your online activity without your awareness. In 2019, ESET even found a trojanized version of Tor Browser that replaced Bitcoin addresses on websites to direct payments to hackers. So both genuine websites and your browser itself are also vulnerable to manipulation if you download or access them from an unverified source.

There are a few best practices to avoid phishing attacks when using the dark web. None of them are foolproof on their own, but together, they considerably lower the risk of ending up on a fake or manipulated website.

On the desktop version of Tor Browser, you can access an onion site using a shortened version of its URL called an Onion Name. For now, this feature only works with SecureDrop, so newsrooms can establish tip lines with addresses like mysitename.securedrop.tor.onion, which would then redirect to the 56-character original onion address. This feature is in active development, so more platforms might support it in the future.

When you load up an onion site using the Tor Browser, you’ll see an onion icon on the address bar, which confirms that your connection is end-to-end encrypted. But you can also click on the onion icon to check if the site has an Extended Validation (EV) certificate, which tells you that its authenticity has been verified by a trusted certificate authority like DigiCert. While not every legitimate onion site will have an EV certificate, famous ones like Facebook tend to.

On the other hand, if you see a caution sign next to the onion icon, that means the site is using a self-signed or expired certificate that isn’t guaranteed by a trusted authority. It may also imply that the site is being served over an insecure URL. This doesn’t definitely tell you it’s a phishing site, but it’s a red flag to watch out for nevertheless.

Don’t rely on search engines, link directories, Reddit threads, or Telegram channels too heavily on the dark web. Once you’re sure you’ve found the onion address for a genuine site, bookmark it so you can access it directly the next time you want to visit.

If you realized that you’ve been the victim of a phishing attempt, the first step is to close the browser window with the fake site and access the real onion address to reset any account passwords you may have accidentally divulged.

Also, generally try to enable two-factor authentication and PGP logins on any dark web account that supports it for added security. And if you downloaded Tor Browser from anywhere other than the official Tor Project site, uninstall it now and grab a fresh copy from the official address.

#3505. Want to Smell Bisexual? A Hit Podcast Has the Perfume for You

You Must Remember This is a podcast dedicated, as its host Karina Longworth says in every intro, to exploring the secret and/or forgotten histories of Hollywood’s first century. Longworth, who is an LA–based writer and film preservationist, usually tells her stories in themed seasons. Those include Erotic 90’s, spanning the introduction of the NC-17 rating to Eyes Wide Shut; Dead Blondes (Marilyn Monroe, Jean Harlow, Veronica Lake); and a whole series exploring the web of connections Charles Manson had to Hollywood. It’s addictive, exhaustively researched, and narrated in a way that is both soothing and trancelike.

Longworth is a native Angeleno who has been writing about film for years. She was a film editor and critic at the LA Weekly for three years until 2012; wrote books on Al Pacino and Meryl Streep; and then started You Must Remember This is 2014. She’s also part of a film-loving couple: her husband of 8 years is the Knives Out writer and director Rian Johnson.

The latest season of the podcast is called The Bisexuals, spotlighting the stories of actors and actresses whose love lives were often much more diverse than anything sanctioned by a studio. One star that the season discusses is Libby Holman, a singer and socialite who married the tobacco heir Zachary Smith Reynolds in 1931. Not only did she have a fruitful sex life with Tallulah Bankhead and Montgomery Clift, but she was known for her signature scent called Jungle Gardenia.

In honor of that bombastic perfume that wafted off of her, Longworth, 46, collaborated with Joey Rosin, who formulated a fragrance, Bisexual. Vanity Fair spoke to Longworth about moviegoing in Los Angeles versus New York, what she smelled like as a teenager, being in grad school in your 40s, and her thoughts about Quentin Tarantino’s film programming.

The interview that follows has been condensed for length and clarity.

Vanity Fair: What was the first perfume you remember wearing?

Karina Longworth: Coco Mademoiselle was really a big deal for me when I was 18, 19. It was one of the first perfumes that I ever knew about. I started with The Body Shop’s Tea Rose oil. I didn’t really have any female adult influences because my mom died when I was 11, and so I had to sort of figure out that whole world.

Have you always wanted to make a perfume? Are you a perfume nerd?

So I never had an ambition to make a perfume, but over the past 10 years, I’ve become really into perfume. I used to rent an office space in the same building as an independent perfumer, Jacqueline Ella Steele, whose brand was called Goest— which doesn’t exist anymore—but she made a perfume called Silent Films. She was the first person I contacted about trying to formulate this perfume. But she’s out of business. So that’s when I started asking around and I got led to Joey Rosin.

I got the idea because, in reading and writing about Libby Holman, there are all these anecdotes of her walking into a room in a cloud of Jungle Gardenia, to the point where, people who were attracted to her were attracted to it, and people who didn’t like her found it so disgusting. I thought there was something really interesting about that, how the same scent could be either attractive or repellent, depending on how you felt about the person wearing it.

What does a bisexual smell like? In this case jungles and gardenia

Personalities, voices and clothes all depend on who’s doing it.

There’s this really incredible anecdote in Patricia Bosworth’s Montgomery Clift biography about how one of Montgomery Clift’s friends was at a party at Treetops, Libby Holman’s estate, and she was looking for the bathroom, and accidentally walked into her bedroom, and the bed was a tangle of white satin sheets, and there’s a giant bottle of barbiturates on the nightstand and everything just reeked of Jungle Gardenia. She was grossed out, but then she also got the impression this is Libby and Monty’s sex lair.

We didn’t try to copy the exact old fragrance. Joey does his research, and he did research into what the original notes were. But we talked about not wanting it to be a slavish copy, and instead just trying to evoke for both of us what jungle would smell like with gardenia, and how that could evoke Libby’s story. And so we played around with adding different types of smoke to it.

I’ve been to Tahiti. I’m trying to think if I’ve ever been to a jungle. We talked a lot about tropical plants and what the dirt would smell like, and the heat. It’s like hot weather almost has a smell. But then pairing that with this kind of old lady scent of gardenia. I went to visit his studio in Brooklyn a few times and he mailed some samples to me in Los Angeles. And by that point, it was like four iterations that were almost exactly the same. So it was just about what was giving me the best vibe.

I was living alone in Rochester, N.Y. in a depressing situation because of the weather and being very alone, having no social life.

But you loved your grad school program, right? I forget the name but I know it’s long.

L. Jeffrey Selznick School of Film Preservation at the George Eastman Museum. I got so much out of the program, but it was grueling, physically, and mentally, and emotionally. It was really difficult to suddenly be living alone in a place where I felt like I had no one I could really talk to.

So you were in an entirely new, but temporary situation.

I started relying on scented candles to improve my mood and to change my mood. If I got home feeling terrible, the fragrance was helpful. I also had nowhere to wear perfume. #3504. The Rings Of Power Season 3's Best Storyline Redeems A Controversial Peter Jackson Idea

Spoilers are never late (nor are they early; they arrive precisely when they mean to), so don't read ahead without first watching Season 3, Episodes 5 and 6 of "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power."

Over halfway into its run, it's clear "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" Season 3 is spectacular whenever Sauron (Charlie Vickers) is on-screen. Indeed, this season is for the baddies, with the Dark Lord's menacing Nazgnagôl making their grand entrance and a thrilling civil war brewing in Númenor.

But it's not all doom and gloom, as Season 3 also introduces the brightest light of hope in Middle-earth: the elven golden retriver Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower). From the moment he shows up, it feels like he's been a part of the show from the start, fitting in perfectly as a strong, funny, flirty elf who has excellent chemistry with Galadriel (Morfydd Clark). Celeborn is the ultimate wife guy, and his relationship with Galadriel is the best romance we've seen in a Middle-earth adventure to date.

Nevertheless, there's trouble in Valinor for these two, as Celeborn has competition for Galadriel's heart. No, not Robert Aramayo's Elrond (despite them sharing a kiss in Season 2 to distract the orcs holding Galadriel captive), but Sauron, the Dark Lord on his dark throne in the Land of Mordor where the Shadows lie.

That's right: "The Rings of Power" Season 3 has finally turned "The Lord of the Rings" into a romantasy story, placing a love triangle at the heart of the saga of the One Ring. And while J.R.R. Tolkien purists may scoff at this, the show's love triangle is so good that it redeems the controversial romances from Peter Jackson's otherwise beloved "Lord of the Rings" films.

Peter Jackson's "Lord of the Rings" films are the most widely celebrated fantasy movies of all time and changed the genre forever. As such, it's easy nowadays to forget that Jackson's trilogy stirred up its fair share of controversy upon its initial release. After all, as faithful as they were to J.R.R. Tolkien's original books overall, those films also made some big alterations. That includes erasing the Scouring of The Shire from "The Return of the King" and removing characters like Tom Bombadil and Glorfindel, in addition to introducing a prominent love triangle.

In Jackson's movies, to jog your memory, a respectable amount of time is spent on Éowyn (Miranda Otto) falling in love with Aragorn (Viggo Mortensen), with even King Théoden (Bernard Hill) buying into their match and congratulating Éowyn on finding a good and honest man. Meanwhile, Aragorn keeps thinking about Arwen (Liv Tyler), who is about to leave Middle-earth for Valinor. In fact, the original plan was for Arwen to be at Helm's Deep alongside Éowyn and Aragorn in "The Two Towers," which presumably would've fueled their love triangle even further.

Things get even worse in Jackson's "The Hobbit" films. There, he and co-writers Philippa Boyens and Fran Walsh introduce Tauriel (Evangeline Lilly), an elf who develops romantic feelings for the dwarf Kili (Aidan Turner). In that case, it's Legolas (Orlando Bloom) who rounds out the love triangle, as he's still racist towards dwarves at the time.

Neither of these Middle-earth love triangles really work (especially not the latter), so it's hard not to be skeptical of "The Rings of Power" introducing yet another one. And yet, this ends up being the most compelling aspect of Season 3.

There are two things that make the love triangle in "The Rings of Power" work. The first is that the show is very clearly in on the joke, with Sauron often behaving like a teenager when it comes to his borderline hilarious fixation on Galadriel. That he even goes to the trouble of disguising himself as Galadriel and kissing Celeborn to get information out of him shows Sauron is not beyond being a little bi-curious.

Then there's the fact that the series has been building to this since Season 1, starting with Galadriel slowly falling for Sauron in disguise as Halbrand and being seduced by his promises of power. By the time Season 3 rolls along, she still has complicated feelings for him, as evidenced by her dreams and visions of Sauron waking up in bed next to her. Thus, when Celeborn re-enters her life, and Galadriel sees both men in front of her, there's a tiny bit of hesitation on her part.

And yet, Season 3 never suggests that Galadriel would actually leave her husband for the Dark Lord. Instead, it juxtaposes Sauron's jealousy with Celeborn's confidence. Specifically, in Episodes 5 and 6, Sauron gets visibly flustered when Celeborn talks about how much Galadriel loves him. In the end, it works just as well as the incredible romances in J.R.R. Tolkien's source material, proving that Middle-earth is not devoid of effective romantic storytelling.

Heck, the scene in Episode 6where Celeborn talks about making the elven smith that Sauron has been looking for tell him the secrets of the rings, just so he can hear about every minute the smith spent with Galadriel, is arguably the most romantic TV scene of 2026. Stream Season 3 on Prime Video, and see for yourself.

SNL might look like a smooth and well-oiled machine to viewers watching the weekly live show at home, but by all accounts, it’s absolute chaos behind the scenes at Studio 8H. In fact, just getting through the show can be such a hectic ordeal for the host that they’re assigned someone to manage their schedule, keep them fed and make sure they’re in the right place and wearing the right costume at the right time. It turns out it’s the same employee every week. Her name is Donna Richards, and she’s apparently seen all the famous people naked.

During a recent episode of Good Hang with Amy Poehler, Richards and her role on the show came up after guest Jack Black talked about her hunting down an Italian chopped salad for him because he was starving between dress rehearsal and the live show. Apparently she’s there to make sure the host is relaxed, comfortable and dressed to perform. Sometimes that means making sure they’ve eaten, and sometimes that means physically yanking clothes on and off them during frantic costume changes between sketches. Here’s a portion of what Poehler said…

She has this really specific job that’s like part nurse, part coach where she kinda grabs you and dresses you from scene to scene. She has your whole show in her hand. She makes sure you can do it. She is the one that if you pass out or you forgot something and turn to her and say I don’t remember, she would have you. She’s your wrangler. She’s seen everybody naked. She’s seen every star naked.

SNL fans are very familiar with the work it takes to pitch, write and rehearse the show every week, but there’s a lot less familiarity around the actual mechanics of making the live show happen. It’s ultimately because of people like Richards and other unsung heroes who make sure their more famous co-workers are physically able to go out there and make us laugh. It’s better for everyone if Jack Black is worried about being funny and not worried about remembering which outfit he’s supposed to get into next and which wig it pairs with.

During the same conversation, Poehler said Richards could write a great book just recounting all of the ridiculous requests that she’s gotten since she started on the show. Apparently, Black asking for an Italian chopped salad without onions is incredibly tame compared to the nonsense she’s normally asked to do, but fortunately, she’s been able to weather those storms and build amazing relationships with cast members and many of the celebrities who have hosted.

Tina Fey made sure she got her moment to appear on camera during SNL’s 50th Anniversary, and she’s been the subject of a bunch of fun interviews like this where cast members and celebrities shout her out. She’s even apparently developed a fun little bond with Jason Momoa who has come and visited her on a few different occasions.

Richards and everyone else working on SNL has a short break from the show for the holidays, but they’ll all return the first week of December for the next episode, which will be guest hosted by Amanda Seyfried. I can’t wait to see what the talented actress is able to see, thanks in part to Richards who will apparently clothe her, feed her and let her exclusively focus on crushing her lines.

#3500. Meta's VR Glasses Could Be The Future Of Home Viewing (But They Probably Won't)

In stark contrast to the dire straits that the movie theater industry was in just a few years ago, 2026 has been especially encouraging to those of us who adore going to the movies. A big part of why that's changed lies in the industry's embrace of unique Premium Large Formats, with numerous releases this year having been shown in formats like IMAX, 4DX, Screen X, Dolby Cinema, and so on. Along the way, screening on celluloid (70mm in particular) have become a draw unto themselves, and some cities are home to even more specialized formats, among them Las Vegas' immersive Sphere and the Cosm experience. And while the biggest draw to movie theaters will always be good films, it's clear that audiences also enjoy an experience they can't get elsewhere.

As usual, however, the tech industry isn't far behind to try and stoke the competition between theaters and home viewing. While most consumers have been content with things like big screen 4K TV's or even their handheld devices for watching at home or on the go, the latest attempt to leap forward from these is just around the corner, in the form of Meta's VR Glasses. It's important to note that these are not the latest version of the smart glasses that have existed on the market since 2021, as they're explicitly not designed to be used while engaged in other activity. Instead, they're a cutting edge virtual/augmented reality system intended to bring together multiple work and entertainment options while idle.

I recently had the opportunity to try these glasses for myself, and their potential, especially for home viewing, is amazing. That said, there are some restrictions to them which, unless changed, mean they won't be replacing our existing personal devices anytime soon.

Although virtual reality, or VR, has existed in some form for decades, it's mostly been utilized as a gimmick more than a viable first choice for media. Fortunately, the folks behind Meta VR Glasses seem to understand this. I got to see a clip from the recent concert doc "Billie Eilish — Hit Me Hard and Soft: The Tour (Live in 3D)" on the glasses, and the experience was like I was watching it on a movie theater screen. That is to say that the aspect ratio was exactly the same as its theatrical exhibition, and the 3D display was pitch perfect. Turning my head in any direction didn't move the "screen," but kept it fixed in front of me, as if it was a physical object in the space, which is a very smart design.

While the James Cameron documentary acted as a demo of how watching most films and shows on the glasses would go, the Meta employees next showed me what they're calling "Enhanced Cinema." Using a clip from "Avengers: Infinity War" in which Thor (Chris Hemsworth) constructs Stormbreaker, the presentation was almost exactly akin to the Cosm experience. This meant that the film was playing on a similar fixed "display" in front of me, while all around me (literally 360 degrees — I checked!) was the environment of the forge on Nidavellir. It's an effect that's totally immersive but not distracting, nor does it betray the original intent of the film itself. After being told that Meta has an exclusive license with the IMAX corporation to present movies filmed for that format on the glasses, I have no doubt that the device could brilliantly replicate those screens for home viewing, and that's incredibly exciting.

While the Meta VR Glasses are not intended to replace a smartphone or similar device, they do seem to do a lot of what those devices do, only bigger and better. From working on VR video games and multiple computer monitors at once to allowing you to watch sports games as they broadcast while seeing the view from courtside, the glasses seem almost too good to be true as a personal media device.

This is where the catches come in. For one thing, watching something with other people at the same time can only occur depending on the content. For another, though they're engineered to be used while stationary, the temptation for people to wear them in public while walking (or, god forbid, driving) exists, and it's quite troubling. Then there's the fact that the glasses seem designed to only work with whatever services and content Meta allows. This means that us physical media fans are SOL, and as with any all-digital service, the content available on the glasses could be subject to change (or disappear) at any time. That's a lot to ask for a device priced at $1,299.99 USD, which is about the same as a new iPhone.

Note: Following publication, a representative for Meta did inform us that the VR glasses will support playback devices that are compatible via a wired DisplayPort-over-USB-C connection, meaning that additional content (like physical media) that the consumer has control over may be viewable on the glasses.

Right now, Meta's killer app beyond the tech itself are its exclusive licenses, such as with IMAX and James Cameron's Lightstorm Entertainment. The only way it'll compete with devices already on the market is if it can consistently deliver the quality experiences I got to have with it while being as user friendly as possible. If the glasses prove they can be used at home and on the go as smoothly as an iPhone can now, then they could be a game changer. Until then, they're just a gimmick, albeit a really nice one.

That extra brightness is useful in rooms with some ambient light, but the tradeoff is louder fan noise.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. #3498. Huge New Nvidia Bug Is Ruining Gaming Hardware, Users Say

Nvidia has not been having a good couple of weeks

Nvidia is in rough shape. As the hardware company scrambles to replace its CEO and co-founder, Jensen Huang, after a series of scandals, it seems the needs of lowly gamers aren’t high on the priority list. Earlier this year, the company ran into controversy over its ugly generative AI-fueled DLSS 5 technology. If you need more evidence that Nvidia is focused on cranking out chips for generative AI rather than supporting its gaming hardware, the company has failed to fix a bug reportedly capable of damaging users’ PCs by writing excessive amounts of data to solid-state drives (SSDs).

The bug was found in the last two driver updates for Nvidia graphics cards — specifically, the 621.14 and 621.24 updates for the Nvidia GeForce Game Ready Driver. The 621.24 update went live on Nov. 12. As first reported by TroubleGrid, the bug causes constant writes (saving data) on a user’s SSD, degrading the hardware while potentially causing stutters and mouse pointer hitches. Specifically, the bug apparently causes NVDisplay.Container.exe to write an excessive amount of information to an Nvidia log file, resulting in as much as 30 GB being written per hour.

While this executable already wrote to log files before the most recent driver update, versions 621.14 and 621.24 can cause dramatically more data to be written. It usually takes years for an SSD to degrade naturally, but the excessive data logged by the Nvidia bug could speed up this process. The bug seems to be causing performance issues for some users as data is written in the background. The easiest fix is to downgrade your graphics card driver to version 621.01, which is the last known patch that didn’t have the problem.

Users have reported the bug on most major PC gaming subreddits, and they’re not happy. “Trying to destroy our computers so we stop hoarding all their RAM,” one user said, referencing a now-infamous quote from OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. “AMD and NVIDIA releasing firmware that prematurely kills SSD’s when SSD’s have become 7x more expensive than they were 18 months ago [thinking emoji],” another wrote, conspiratorially implying that these bugs were deliberately created to damage users’ computers and make them buy expensive new SSDs. “Makes you wonder if it’s AI code incompetence or a concerted effort to kill personal computing,” someone else replied.

As this comment suggests, some have suggested that the bug may be a byproduct of Nvidia’s increasing use of AI-generated code. Earlier this year, Huang said he wanted his developers to use AI chatbots and agents more often to help with programming. In that context, this bug may be a Hanlon’s razor situation rather than a conspiracy: "Never attribute to malice that which is adequately explained by stupidity."

Ugly AI graphics and a 50% performance hit, what's not to love?

#3497. 10 Years Ago Today: The Harry Potter Universe Expanded With A Star-Studded Spin-Off

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

"Harry Potter" is perhaps the defining franchise of the 2000s, but all good things must come to an end. That end originally came in 2011 with "Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows – Part 2" which had the biggest opening ever up to that point in cinema history. But creator J.K. Rowling and Warner Bros. weren't content to let the Wizarding World end there. Ten years ago, they expanded the universe with a star-studded spin-off.

Set decades before Harry Potter was even born, 2016's "Fantastic Beasts and Where to Find Them," which opened 10 years ago today, brought the action to America and focused on entirely new characters within the Wizarding World. Specifically Newt Scamander, played by Oscar-winner Eddie Redmayne. Redmayne had an unexpected inspiration for his performance, namely film icon Buster Keaton. The movie itself was loosely based on an in-universe textbook mentioned in the main series, with Rowling eventually releasing a version of the book, though it didn't contain a narrative.

The resulting prequel/spin-off takes place in 1926 centered on magizoologist Newt Scamander as he arrives in New York during a worldwide tour to research and rescue magical creatures. A mysterious magical being begins causing chaos in NYC, which threatens to expose the wizarding world to the muggles of Earth.

Redmayne was far from the only big star to secure a role in the spin-off. The stacked cast also includes but is not limited to Katherine Waterston, Dan Fogler, Alison Sudol, Samantha Morton, Ezra Miller, and Colin Farrell. "Fantastic Beats" also cast Johnny Depp as Grindelwald in a surprise appearance. Arguably the most important casting decision the movie made, with the benefit of hindsight.

J.K. Rowling wrote the script for "Fantastic Beasts and Where to Find Them" personally, which wasn't the case with the other "Harry Potter" movies. David Yates, who helmed the final four "Harry Potter" movies, was recruited to tackle the spin-off as well, providing a sturdy hand.

The majority of the core cast were on the upswing. This movie was expected to be a big break for all of them. In many ways, it was. "Fantastic Beasts" was dubbed a worthy extension of the Wizarding World in many reviews, with audiences tending to agree. Even if it wasn't effusive praise, it was good enough.

The movie was released in November 2016 and did quite well for itself, pulling in $816 million at the global box office. That was more than enough to convince Warner Bros. to double down, with four "Fantastic Beasts" sequels announced before the first one even hit theaters. Everyone involved fully expected this to be the long-term future for the "Harry Potter" franchise. What's perhaps most surprising about that, especially in light of the first movie's success, is the fact that the words Harry Potter don't appear anywhere in the title. All the same, audiences found it.

The train had left the station and everyone involved had every reason to believe, on paper, that people would show up for the sequels en masse. After all, the first installment scored well enough with critics and was the eighth-biggest movie of 2016 overall. Unfortunately, the future had different plans.

Warner Bros. and director David Yates wasted no time, with the second "Fantastic Beasts" installment dated for November 2018. Much of the cast returned, with new additions entering the fold. But in no small part due to forces beyond the studio's control, "The Crimes of Grindelwald" doomed "Fantastic Beasts."

The sequel pulled in more than $650 million at the box office, but made a lot less domestically and had to rely on international audiences to bail it out. Then there's the Depp of it all. Controversy started swirling around the actor due to his public feud with his ex-wife Amber Heard, involving accusations of domestic abuse. Depp later dropped out of the "Fantastic Beasts" franchise following a court case verdict. Mads Mikkelsen took over as Grindelwald in "The Secrets of Dumbledore," but the writing was on the wall.

The third installment made hardly more than $400 million globally, failing to break even theatrically. "The Secrets of Dumbledore" proved that the magic was gone, despite the appeal of Jude Law as a younger Albus Dumbledore in a lead role. The cast continued to be star-studded all along the way but, at a certain point, appealing casts only go so far. Especially in the 2020s when audiences are more content than ever to stay at home and stream something from the couch.

Controversy and middling results with diminishing returns eventually derailed "Fantastic Beasts." Ten years ago though, the spin-off arrived with a great deal of promise and a lot of potential. That potential just never proved out.

You can grab "Fantastic Beasts and Where to Find Them" on 4K, Blu-ray, or DVD from Amazon.

#3496. Avengers: Doomsday's PG-13 Rating Explained

We are a month away from potentially the biggest box office weekend of 2026, with Dunesday set to blow Barbenheimer out of the water as both "Dune: Part Three" and "Avengers: Doomsday" make their way into theaters. These movies are aimed at similar audiences, yet they're vastly different when it comes to their tones and approaches to adapting popular characters for the big screen. Indeed, where Denis Villeneuve's cinematic takes on the "Dune" books have so far been somber and introspective, the road to "Doomsday" has been paved almost entirely with nostalgia.

To be sure, between Robert Downey Jr. returning to the Marvel Cinematic Universe (this time to play Doctor Doom), the latest Avengers roster featuring multiple beloved characters from the MCU's past, and several actors reprising their roles from 20th Century Fox's "X-Men" films, "Doomsday" has had no problem catching the attention and interest of virtually every kind of moviegoer out there. After all, where "Dune: Part Three" can afford to target older audiences given the mature themes of its source material, "Doomsday" is aimed at everyone with a pulse and a heartbeat.

Hence, it's no surprise to learn that the new "Avengers" movie is now officially rated PG-13, just like almost every other previous film entry in the MCU since 2008 (save for "Deadpool & Wolverine"). Per FilmRatings.com, the film earned this rating from the Motion Picture Association (MPA) based on its "violence/action, bloody images, and language."

Just in case it needs to be said, "Avengers: Doomsday" was never going to be rated anything other than PG-13. The MCU's movies, in general, tend to feature too much intense action for any of them to garner a mere PG rating, yet they also tend to avoid going overboard into full-blown adult territory. At the same time, the explanation for its rating suggests "Doomsday" will make good on its promise of being one of the darker installments in the franchise.

Keeping that in mind, Marvel Studios and Disney were never going to allow a movie as costly as this one to get slapped with an R rating either, lest it severely limit the number of people who can pay to see it in a theater. And yes, "Deadpool & Wolverine" managed to become a massive success with an R-rating, but that was a different situation. Since the first two "Deadpool" films had been R-rated, it might've actually hurt the movie financially if it had tried to take the larger "Deadpool" property in a more family-friendly direction.

That's not to suggest that "Doomsday" won't be sufficiently dark or violent, though. Just too long ago, in fact, Sam Raimi pushed the PG-13 rating as far as humanly possible with 2022's "Doctor Strange In the Multiverse of Madness," the most gruesome Marvel movie yet. As you may recall, that film was filled with incredibly brutal death scenes, legitimate jump scares, and upsetting imagery that's not suitable for younger audiences. On the other hand, we can probably safely assume "Doomsday" won't push the envelope that far, given everything that's riding on it.

You can see what "Avengers: Doomsday" has to offer for yourself when it opens in theaters on December 18, 2026.

As you get older, a strong core becomes even more important to help you maintain balance and stability and avoid injury. But the types of core exercises you enjoyed at 20 might not be the types you enjoy today, and for me personally, at 35, I now prefer low-impact, deep core exercises over typical moves like sit-ups, crunches, or planks.

For that reason, I wanted to share one exercise I love for strengthening your core and hips while remaining low-impact for your spine.

One of the best core exercises I use with my dad, who is nearing 73, looks simple but really blasts your core and deep stabilizer muscles. It also strengthens your hip flexors, which are important muscles for walking and running. Read on to learn more.

As a reminder, this exercise is beginner-friendly. Still, if you're pregnant, postpartum, or dealing with an injury, it’s always best to seek personalized advice from an expert who knows you and your body.

I like exercises that keep your spine straight and stable while teaching the various muscles that form your core to maintain and control tension. So, rather than peddling out endless sit-ups, which flex your spine over and over, I recommend trying leg openers.

If you're unsure what "bracing" your core means, I teach you how with a 5-minute bracing routine.

Here’s how to perform leg openers with proper form:

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

A post shared by Tom's Guide Fitness | Workout Tips & Gear (@tomsguidefitness)

Avoid hunching or dumping into your torso. Imagine a piece of string running along your spine and coming out of the crown of your head. Now imagine someone pulling that string to lift you.

Move slowly and with control, using your braced stomach to maintain your upright position. You can slightly lean back, but try not to do so excessively.

Yes, which is why I use it with older clients regularly. The move teaches proper posture and spinal alignment as you keep your shoulders stacked over your hips and avoid hunching or rounding. This also requires your core muscles to activate to hold you upright and keep you stable; a strong, active core protects your lower back.

Leg openers also work your hip flexors, which are important muscles for lifting your knees, allowing you to walk and run. As you abduct the hip, your outer glutes and adductors also switch on; your glutes help stabilize the pelvis, and the adductors run along your inner thighs, sometimes referred to as the groin.

This exercise is much friendlier for your lower back than moves like sit-ups, as you can support your lower back if needed, and you don't need to use any extreme range of motion, like hyperextension or flexion, or spinal compression. This move also teaches you to control the movement you generate, increasing time under tension, or how long your muscles work, to build endurance.

I like to count four seconds out with a one-second pause and a four-second count back in. If you notice you're leaning back too much, position yourself against a wall to prevent this, as you want to maintain a strong L-shaped position with your body. A soft bend in the working leg is fine if you have tight hamstrings.

#3492. Avengers: The Kang Dynasty's Scrapped Doctor Doom Twist Explained By Marvel's Kevin Feige

As we march ever closer to "Avengers: Doomsday," it's easy to forget this movie was supposed to look very different. The original lead-in to "Avengers: Secret Wars" was supposed to be "Avengers: The Kang Dynasty," as directed by Destin Daniel Cretton (who had already helmed "Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings" for Marvel and would go on to direct "Spider-Man: Brand New Day").

Kang the Conqueror (Jonathan Majors), a time traveler who hails from the 31st century, appeared as the main villain of "Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania." A post-credits scene debuted the "Council of Kangs," or all of Kang's variants from a multiverse full of different timelines. But "Quantumania" earned unenthusiastic reviews upon its release in February 2023, and worse, Majors was arrested for assault the following month. (He was found guilty, and then fired by Marvel/Disney, in December 2023.)

Yeah, not exactly the launching pad you want for your next Thanos. Cue a pivot, and the announcement at San Diego Comic-Con 2024 that "Kang Dynasty" had been reworked into "Avengers: Doomsday," featuring Robert Downey Jr. returning to Marvel but as Doctor Doom, not Iron Man, as well as the return of "Infinity War" and "Endgame" directors Joe and Anthony Russo.

Now, this all seems like a "break glass in case of emergency" situation. But Marvel Studios President Kevin Feige, sitting down with Empire Magazine, now claims that even before "The Kang Dynasty" became "Doomsday," Kang was planned to be a red herring for Doom:

"People think there was a cause-and-effect with Jonathan's issues, and that certainly accelerated some things. But the Doom of it all was well underway before that. [...] It probably would still have been called 'The Kang Dynasty,' but it would have been a set-up for Doom, midway through that movie."

Kevin Feige, noting the "very delicate" situation with Jonathan Majors, told Empire that "[Marvel] didn't want to rush into any rash decisions in terms of employment." He acknowledged the changes to "The Kang Dynasty" started after the bad reception and underperformance of "Quantumania," noting:

"'Quantumania' was not received the way we would have liked. There are many elements of that that we're proud of, the Kang performance being one of them. But we were changing [The Kang Dynasty] even at that point."

Reading between the lines of Feige's claims, it would appear that once Majors was fired, the studio decided to push forward with Doom as the villain from the start instead of recasting Kang. But is this credible? I'll admit my first thought while reading this was, "Yeah, right!"

In his Empire interview, Feige appears to say the plans to bring in Doom to supplant Kang happened after the release of "Quantumania" but before Majors' arrest. "Quantumania" was released on February 17, 2023, and Majors was arrested on March 25, 2023. That seems like a pretty slim window to rework "The Kang Dynasty."

In November 2023, Variety reported that — at the annual Marvel Studios retreat held that past September — studio leadership was actively discussing how to move forward with Kang. ("Marvel is truly f***ed with the whole Kang angle," an insider was quoted as saying.) Apparently, the Marvel brain trust discussed replacing Kang with another villain, Doom specifically being named, as well as bringing back Avengers who died in "Endgame," like Robert Downey Jr. as Iron Man, to gin up excitement. As we now know, that's basically what Marvel did.

During a November 2023 appearance on the "Hot Mic" podcast, journalist Jeff Sneider claimed that Doom would appear in the then-upcoming "The Fantastic Four: First Steps" (which he did) as set up for him to show up in "Avengers: Secret Wars." However, Sneider said in that same interview that, "It'd be inaccurate to say [Doom is] the villain."

But Doom is the villain of Marvel Comics overall. The only reason the Marvel Cinematic Universe waited so long to use him is because 20th Century Fox held the film rights to his character. Once the Disney and Fox merger was completed in 2019, and Doom became available to Marvel Studios, Doom had to be high on any list of characters being considered for inclusion.

The "Secret Wars" comics — both the 1984 original and the 2015 pseudo-remake — also feature Doom as the main villain. In both, he attains godlike power and rules over a domain called Battleworld. If you're adapting "Secret Wars," the thought of using Doom has to cross your mind.

Kevin Feige's claim that Doom would take over "midway" through "The Kang Dynasty" also aligns with supposed leaked plot summaries for "Doomsday," which assert that Doom initially presents himself as an ally before revealing his true intentions. If that's accurate, it appears the movie still has the broad structure of "The Kang Dynasty," just with no Kang.

On the other hand, "Secret Wars" (especially the 2015 one) is a culmination of Doom's character. Rushing right into him becoming a God Emperor of Battleworld, without him being the villain in a "Fantastic Four" movie first? Yeah, that sounds like something that was "accelerated," per Feige.

"Avengers: Doomsday" releases on December 18, 2026.

Here, players participate in collaborative missions in order to build a prize fund. But it's not all fun and games: There's a secret double agent among the group (the mole, obviously) whose sole task is to undermine the ability of the rest of the group to earn money. Eliminations are done via quiz: The group is grilled on the information they've collected about the mole, and whoever knows the least gets the boot. Originally airing in the aughts, Netflix brought it back for a couple of seasons more recently, with the potential for more to come. Stream the most recent seasons of The Mole on Netflix.

If there were a prize for dramatic title (and set design), you could do a lot worse than this one. In this South Korean reality show, 12 celebrity contestants are challenged to build a prize pot through strategy games. Sometimes they're collaborative, sometimes entirely competitive, and sometimes a blend, but prizes come in the form of "Pieces" that can be won or lost (and that eventually combine to create their own final puzzle). Anyone who finds themselves without a single Piece is out. Pieces can be spent to buy advantages, and also traded, so the show turns on players forming alliances in order to build the prize pot and survive as long as possible. Stream The Devil's Plan on Netflix.

Here, a bunch of strangers are holed up in an apartment building, cut off from the outside world—and each other. Players can only interact via a custom app, and, thus, can portray themselves however they want, whether that means being 100% genuine (unlikely!) or creating a whole new persona. Players judge the competition based on their interactions, determining the "Influencers" who will get to decide on the eliminations. The show ran for seven seasons on Netflix, and is moving to Hulu for the forthcoming eighth. Stream The Circle on Hulu.

You show up at a fancy hotel, and someone hands you a suitcase containing one million dollars. It's yours to keep—as long as you can keep it a secret. In this one, all the contestants get a suitcase, and only one contains the money. Much as with The Traitors, the goal is to figure out who's keeping the secret, with challenges designed to help flush that person out. If the truth is discovered via a vote, that former millionaire is ousted and the money is concealed in another suitcase until the final contestants are given the opportunity to swap bags with someone who they think has the money. Easy come, easy go, I guess. Stream Million Dollar Secret on Netflix.

I'm a little more into the normies on Traitors myself, but there's no question that a big part of the appeal (for most seasons) is watching reality-show celebs go at it with cash on the line. So it is with House of Villains, a Big Brother-style competition with Joel McHale as ringmaster. The core premise is pretty simple: villains (Richard Hatch, Tom Sandoval, Jonny Fairplay, one-time Trump bestie Omarosa Newman, etc.) compete in challenges for rewards and for safety from the inevitable banishment. It's all mostly an excuse to watch some of TV's biggest personalities go for each other's jugulars. Stream House of Villains on Peacock.

This is not a reality show, but rather a drama about a reality show that may well slake your thirst for treachery while offering up consequences a bit more dramatic than the bruised egos and hurt feelings of The Traitors. Here, eight strangers are selected to compete in a game in which they're locked together in a building and sequestered on different floors each night. They earn money for each minute they last in the game, but all their provisions must be purchased with money they've won, at an extreme markup. At first, the contestants pool their resources so that everyone gets more money—until they learn that people on higher floors are getting more. Then things get nasty Stream The 8 Show on Netflix.

This one plays a bit like The Traitors in reverse: A $250,000 prize pot is, right off the bat, allocated to all 11 contestants who get to hang out in a luxurious villa. So the game isn't about winning money so much as it is about how much you'll keep and how much you're willing to share. Eliminations offer the opportunity to remove those who the others don't want to share with—though contestants don't have to actually ever vote anyone out. They can just keep their portion of the money and hang out, something that obviously does not happen. Challenges along the way force contestants to reveal embarrassing and sometimes ugly truths about themselves that may well put them on the outs with the others. There's only one season at present, though there's potential for more. Stream The Trust on Netflix.

Blending the Big Brother-esque social aspects of Traitors with Survivor's love of the great outdoors, this one drops four teams of four into the Alaskan wilderness (moving to Panama for season three). The contestants are all, by inclination, loners, but the game has only one core rule: Only a team (of at least two) can win, so while the game has the typical reality show eliminations, these wilderness enthusiasts must work together in order to take the money. In the same way that The Traitors creates a tension between competition and cooperation via its communal prize pot, Outlast sees its contestants forced to maintain relationships whether they like it or not. Stream Outlast on Netflix.

The tasks on Traitors aren't typically the most thrilling part of the show, which makes this James Bond-branded competition a solid match if you want more complicated and better developed challenges. In this one, nine teams of two visit exotic locations in each episode and compete in spy-themed activities with the ultimate goal of winning £1 million by making it to the end. It leaves out the bits where people sit around a castle strategizing, but it includes, like Traitors, a dapper Scotsman not afraid to camp it up—in this case, Brian Cox, serving as the spymaster who directs the teams in their missions. Stream 007: Road to a Million on Prime Video.

Squid Game: The Challenge would probably be a more reasonable choice for this list—given that it's a proper reality show and not a blood-chilling thriller. But I'm sticking with the original drama here since, as perfectly entertaining as that spin-off is, it feels like it misses the point. In the original (surprise smash hit) drama, 454 needy contestants are recruited for a new reality competition in which they're tasked to play rather simple children's games—with deadly consequences that are cheered on by the wealthy financiers who are willing to pay good money to watch both the poors go at each other, as people turn on each other to survive and to win the rather shockingly large prize. A bit like The Traitors if all of Alan's murder schtick were literally true. Stream Squid Game on Netflix.
