#3490. Where Are the Women? Zero Female Directors on Blumhouse Atomic’s Theatrical Slate for 2027

Blumhouse Atomic put a number on just about everything at its “Business of Fear” press conference on Wednesday. The merged and renamed horror studio put its share of this year’s worldwide horror box office at more than 50 percent.

It has 10 movies scheduled to open nationwide in 2027. Six are originals. Four are new franchise entries. Seven come from “emerging voices,” including three first-time feature filmmakers. At the end of the day’s first panel, IndieWire asked Jason Blum about a number that didn’t make the slides: How many of those 10 movies were directed by women? Zero.

“So we are working with a lot of women,” Blum said after running through several names. “They didn’t fall in next year’s slate.” The Blumhouse founder and CEO added that it was “very, very important to make sure that the directors reflect our audience and look like our audience, so we’re always making a big effort to make sure that that happens.” Related Stories ‘Bedford Park’ Trailer: Sundance Winner Stars Moon Choi, Who Falls for the Other Driver in Her Mother’s Car Accident David Ellison on Elon Musk’s Skydance Investment, Trump and ‘Rush Hour 4,’ and Whether He Would’ve Made ‘Digger’

It was the last question, and neither Atomic Monster founder James Wan nor Blumhouse president Abhijay Prakash expanded on Blum’s answer. Blumhouse Television president Melissa Aouate then took the microphone to moderate the second conversation.

She was the only woman onstage across both discussions, and though Blum had just cited “Scarpetta” showrunner Liz Sarnoff in his answer to IndieWire, Aouate went on to interview four men, including another company president, about their work while no one asked about hers.

In a later statement to IndieWire, Aouate said she welcomed the chance to bring television into a conversation largely about film and wanted to find “more connective tissue between our film and television slates.”

“By most measures, opportunities for women have contracted in so many areas of the industry, and we take that very seriously,” she said, citing Sarnoff on “Scarpetta,” Cynthia Childs on the “Worst Ever” franchise, and Emma Tammi on “Five Nights at Freddy’s” as examples of major women storytellers working at the company.

“The industry still has a long way to go, and so do we,” she said. “That’s work we take seriously, and we’re all working to see our slate reflect it.”

A Blumhouse Atomic spokesperson told IndieWire that women directed 25 percent of the company’s 2026 film slate. The spokesperson did not specify which titles or release formats counted toward that figure, but both 2026 films Blum cited onstage at least premiered at home.

“We had ‘The Last Kiss’ by a female director,” Blum said of Yoko Okumura, whose film debuted in September, shortly after Kate Dolan’s “SOULM8TE” went straight to digital in August. Blum nodded to that project, too, and he also mentioned Tammi, who got a nationwide theatrical release for “Five Nights at Freddy’s” in 2023 before getting hired back for its 2025 sequel.

By the company’s own accounting, that second gig made obvious financial sense.

Prakash plainly explained on Wednesday that when Blumhouse Atomic calculates a return on investment, it divides worldwide ticket sales by the production budget. The first “Freddy’s” earned nearly $300 million worldwide on a reported $20 million budget, while 2025’s “Five Nights at Freddy’s 2” brought in another $240 million against a $51 million budget. By Prakash’s formula, the two films grossed roughly 7.6 times their combined costs.

IndieWire counted 27 features from Blumhouse and Atomic Monster that played in at least 600 U.S. theaters from 2021 through 2025. Our review counted co-productions once and included the first “Five Nights at Freddy’s,” which debuted simultaneously on Peacock.

Still, women helmed only two, and Tammi directed both. (Asked whether she would return for a third “Freddy’s” film, a Blumhouse Atomic spokesperson told IndieWire, “No updates to share on the next installment of ‘Five Nights at Freddy’s’ at this time.”)

Looking back to streaming, there’s a meaningful difference in opportunity for women. Over the same five years, 22 features from Blumhouse and the former Atomic Monster debuted in the U.S. via streaming, premium TV, or digital on demand without a theatrical run. Women directed or co-directed nine of those projects, accounting for roughly 41 percent of films. That’s compared with 7 percent of the companies’ nationwide theatrical releases.

“Obsession” and “Backrooms,” of course, came up repeatedly. Curry Barker’s indie topped the company’s horror chart with more than $500 million worldwide. Kane Parsons’ feature adaptation of his YouTube series earned another $400 million. “Indie horror is suddenly performing as well or better than studio horror,” Blum said. A decade ago, he estimated, those same movies “would’ve made $25 million at the box office.”

He further credited Barker’s years on YouTube with teaching him how to read an audience, noting he’s producing Barker’s second feature, “Anything but Ghosts,” due out next May. Wan also remembered an early Zoom with Parsons, who was young enough that his dad was on the call then.

By the time IndieWire asked where women fit into the 2027 slate, Blum and Wan had thoroughly detailed what they saw in these two young men and how they helped each grow. On the second panel, Aouate asked Atomic Monster president Michael Clear what it takes for a new director to get his attention. He described what he tells agents about someone who hasn’t directed a horror scene.

“It doesn’t mean I might not work with them in the future, but have them go direct a scare in their apartment at two minutes. That’s what we want,” he said. Of Parsons’ “Backrooms” short, he recalled, “It scared me, and that was it.”

The company didn’t say how often shorts directed by women reach decision-makers like Clear. But asked how Blumhouse Atomic seeks out women directors these days, a spokesperson cited “traditional channels and less obvious ones, like our Screamwriting Lab and the horror shorts and online talent our team scouts.”

One woman whose work has caught their attention online is Heidi Wong, who built a following of millions telling illustrated horror stories on TikTok. Last month at New York Comic Con, Wong and Blum announced a deal to develop short films together. Her social media success seems to make her exactly the kind of emerging talent Blumhouse Atomic wants to cultivate. Whether that partnership leads to a theatrical feature remains to be seen.

Eight years ago, Blum apologized after telling Polygon that fewer women were inclined to direct horror movies. In response, researcher Stephen Follows examined three decades of feature films released in U.S. theaters, from 1988 through 2017. Women accounted for just 5.9 percent of horror directors in his sample. Importantly, that figure tells us who got a film into theaters. It says very little about who wanted to make one or how close they came.

Of course, the disparity extends beyond horror. Across all genres last year, women accounted for 13 percent of directors among the 250 highest-grossing films at the domestic box office. That’s down from 16 percent in 2024, per San Diego State University’s Celluloid Ceiling report.

Blumhouse Atomic also has six distribution partners on its 2027 slate. Plus, films that ultimately premiere at home may have been developed with theaters in mind. The same company spokesperson emphasized to IndieWire that women on the company’s creative team often find and develop major movies, too, running some of the brand’s most beloved franchises.

Over the five years IndieWire examined, though, Tammi was still the only woman to direct a Blumhouse movie that reached horror audiences in theaters nationwide. Yes, those 10 release dates for next year could be an accident of timing, with real gender parity just around the corner. But years of women getting fewer chances to scare audiences on the big screen suggest something more enduring than a scheduling coincidence. For a business built on knowing what scares people, Hollywood’s horror industry seems remarkably unafraid of shutting women out.

#3489. The Next Major Fantasy Franchise Has Been Brewing For Over 30 Years

Every new fantasy movie wants to be the next "Lord of the Rings," and every new fantasy TV series wants to be the next "Game of Thrones." But both mediums are littered with the corpses of projects that failed to capture the zeitgeist. That includes perfect little gems like "Dungeons & Dragons: Honor Among Thieves" (whose box office underperformance remains a crushing shame) and "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" (which has proven it's not easy to be "Game of Thrones" for a "Lord of the Rings" audience, even with a billion dollar budget).

Recently, you may have noticed a new fantasy franchise waiting in the wings. Well, "new" isn't the proper word, perhaps — millions of people are very familiar with it. But rather, new to the people who made "Lord of the Rings" and "Game of Thrones" a crossover success. I'm talking about Magic: The Gathering, the long-running fantasy card game that's been draining wallets and firing up imaginations since its debut in 1993, which is now poised to make the leap to the big and small screens with two different projects.

The first of them is a Netflix animated series called "Planeswalker" from showrunner Terry Matalas, who's already a geek favorite thanks to his strong work on "Star Trek: Picard" season 3 and Marvel's "VisionQuest." The second is a live-action feature film starring Maya Hawke from Legendary Pictures and Matt Johnson, the eclectic filmmaker behind titles as divergent as "Blackberry" and "Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie." It's the kind of two-pronged attack that suggests the timing is right for Magic, the biggest fish in its fantasy tabletop pond, to leap into the mainstream ocean.

Magic is about to have its crossover moment, and I think it has the goods to back it up.

Despite being an avid tabletop gamer and RPG player for over 20 years, I'm new to Magic, having only started playing and collecting this year to prepare for the new "Star Trek" set. However, the game got its hooks in me something fierce, and what was intended to be a brief dalliance has transformed into a new hobby/obsession/addiction.

I was initially drawn to the gameplay and its time-tested mechanics: simple to learn, hard to master, and infinitely flexible to match the style you find most entertaining. But the more time I spent in gaming shops, reading the flavor text at the bottom of a particularly dangerous card, noticing recurring characters across years of art, or chatting with people who have been collecting and playing for decades, I found myself increasingly interested in the world behind the game. Specifically, I was drawn to how the game's definition of fantasy was malleable, willing to blend traditional sword-and-sorcery with traditional folklore, gothic horror, science fiction, nautical adventure, and even zany swings like weird Westerns and multidimensional racing. If there's a creative itch to be scratched, the "planeswalkers" who anchor the narrative will surely expose a new world that will do the job nicely.

It's a universe where anything feels possible, starring varied and instantly recognizable heroes and villains who can travel between vastly different worlds as they journey on epic quests. It's a grand canvas with 33 years of history, characters, lore, and storytelling to build upon. There's more than enough for a movie series and TV show to draw on while still having enough to branch out indefinitely from there.

Following the formal announcement of "Planeswalker" at MagicCon, I asked the clerk at a local gaming shop if he was invested in Magic: The Gathering's world or if he just liked playing the game. He was emphatic: the gameplay hooked him, but the world and the characters and the expansive narrative is what kept him coming back. He spoke of the characters and their world with a reverence I've seen others bring to "Star Wars" and similarly rich universes.

The thin line separating the corners of various fantasy fandoms has eroded. The countless fans who line up for Sarah J. Maas novels and the nerds who crack open Magic booster packs aren't quite a circle, but it's a Venn diagram with a lot of overlap. The kind of weirdo fantasy that is Magic's bread and butter is now mainstream. The timing has never been better to open the door to the people devouring fantasy in other mediums and make it clear that the world of Magic: The Gathering is for them, too.

In recent years, Magic has (sometimes controversially) brought in outside franchises like Final Fantasy, Marvel, and yes, "Star Trek," to entice new players to play the game via their "Universe Beyond" label. I can attest firsthand that this works. But Magic is a great game and a rich world. The main draw for new fans shouldn't be just familiar IP on a Magic card. It should be the original world, fleshed out over three decades, itself. That's where a first-rate movie or show can do the heavy lifting.

The people who go to movie theaters every week and scroll the Netflix Top 10 every night may not realize that Magic offers a world as deep as Middle-earth or Westeros. The film and TV show must treat this universe itself as the main event, the reason to hit play or buy a ticket. A Magic: The Gathering series or movie will need more than just its players to be a true success ... and all of those new viewers pulled into a compelling fantasy epic become potential new players once they realize the game offers more of what they see on their screen.

If this film and this show are good (and they've certainly rounded up some promising talent), the Magic universe could be the next obsession for fantasy movie and TV fans. Even those who have never stepped into a gaming shop in their lives.

#3488. Five Things I Wish I'd Known Before Getting a Foldable Phone

The iPhone Duo might be the highest profile foldable phone to date, but it’s by no means the first. Personally, I’ve had my eye on the Google variant, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold—and recently I finally took the plunge. I thought I’d done my research to know how different having a foldable phone would be, but I still had a bit to learn. Here are some of the things I wish I’ve learned along the way after making the jump to foldables.

One of the most notable aspects of the iPhone Duo is how wide its screen is, even while closed. And there’s a good reason for that: The larger screen while open has exactly the same 1.41:1 aspect ratio as the smaller screen while closed. This has a ripple effect on how every app you use looks and feels—and whether you like Apple’s approach is largely a matter of personal preference.

Compare with my Pixel 11 Pro Fold, which features an extremely tall 2.17:1 aspect ratio when closed, but a nearly square 1:04:1 aspect ratio when open. On the outer screen, apps are a little less wide than on my old phone, but there’s plenty of space for reading books or articles on the inner screen.

I like the tall, thin display personally because it feels easier to reach buttons with my thumb, and the wider display is better for reading. However, this approach can occasionally result in some odd app layouts. Not every app is designed for tablets, especially on Android, and shifting the aspect ratio between the inner and outer display sometimes means re-rendering or even restarting an app entirely to load properly.

The iPhone Duo has a more consistent aspect ratio and general feel between the inner and outer display, but it comes at the cost of a really wide phone. Neither approach is better or worse on its own, but it might be worth going to a local store to get your hands on the phone you’re thinking about before buying.

For years, the screens on most smartphones have been made of increasingly tough and scratch-resistant glass. So tough that you might not even need a screen protector anymore. On a foldable phone, that can be true of the outside display, but it’s very much not when it comes to the inner, foldable display.

Screens might be foldable, but the strong, durable glass that makes your phone so scratch-resistant isn’t. No matter what foldable phone you use, the covering on the inner display will be more flexible, and thus softer. Apple uses a nano-texture polymer film that can be replaced, but the film on most foldable phones cannot. That means if they get damaged or scratched, those marks will be there for the life of your phone.

If you (like me) haven’t considered a screen protector in a while, it might be time to try one again, at least for the inner display. It’s also worth keeping in mind how rough you plan to be with your phone. Construction sites or factories might not be the best home for a foldable phone you plan to open a lot, but an office job should be a bit safer.

Similar to the screen protector issue, cases can be more of a headache. Most rigid cases will come in two pieces, and the piece that covers the outer display can be shockingly minimal—barely more than a frame, for some of the cases I looked at. A poorly made case can be brittle or pop off more easily, so it’s more important to get a high-quality one.

If you like to use your phone case as your wallet, it’s also important to be wary of cases that aren’t specifically designed for your model of phone (and maybe some that are). A lot of wallet cases are built to unfold to reveal your phone’s screen on one side, and your cards and ID on the other. But depending on how your foldable phone unfolds, it could be awkward to reach the inner screen.

The hinge also introduces more spaces for dust and debris to get into your phone. Despite the extra moving parts and gaps, most foldable phones still offer the now-standard IP68 dust and water resistance rating. That mainly applies to what can get inside and damage the components inside your phone. It’s still possible for hair and dirt to get gummed up in any pinchable spaces, so look out for any case that might provide even more nooks for dust to collect in.

I’ve set up most of my apps how I like them by now, but when I first got my foldable phone, I had to revisit some settings I thought I was done messing with. One of the most notable examples was my ebook apps: I was previously using a single-column, medium-font layout, but it looked ridiculous on the inner display. After switching to a two-column layout, it not only felt more natural, but a lot like reading a regular book.

Similarly, there were some uses for my calendar app that got a whole lot more useful. I’ve never really been able to use anything other than either the one-day or Schedule view if I want to make out anything, but on the inner screen, I can finally look at my week at a glance. But that meant tweaking some things—like showing reminders, which fit naturally amid my events in Schedule view, but become a cluttered mess when I saw 14 different reminders to take my meds at once in the Week view.

Most apps do a decent job of automatically adjusting to different screen sizes, but I found a few outliers that I had to figure out myself. As an example, Google Docs would default to a view with extremely tiny text when I first started using it. It took me a bit to figure out that this was due to a “Print layout” toggle in the document’s settings. This is, for some reason, enabled by default when opening a document on the larger inner screen. It can take some time to learn the eccentricities of all your apps, but it’s worth poking around when you can.

I know, it sounds so obvious, right? The outer screen is the one you’ll use most often, so how could you forget about it? But when you unfold the inner screen, the outer one is still useful in some surprising ways that I hadn’t even considered until I went poking around in some of my apps.

One of the most adorable examples is the Made You Look feature in the Pixel’s Camera app. When unfolded, you can take a picture using the rear camera and see a preview like normal, while the outer screen shows silly animations to capture the attention of a baby or toddler that you want to look into the camera. Admittedly, this is an older feature, but it’s a clever one. For adults, you can also use the outer display to get a selfie preview while using the rear-facing camera.

The outer screen is also just better for some things. YouTube is one of the few apps that has a unique layout designed for a partially folded screen, with the video playing on the tilted-up portion of the screen, and video controls on the bottom portion.

However, in my experience, it was a lot nicer to watch a YouTube video by just propping up the outer screen by unfolding the phone a bit, like a kickstand. My Pixel even detected when YouTube was in full-screen mode on the outer display and would be more forgiving of unfolding the phone without switching to the inner screen. The phone anticipated I might just want to prop up the smaller screen, which I thought was a nice touch.

#3487. Quentin Tarantino's Near-Perfect New Netflix Thriller Could Be the Next 'Knives Out'

The uncanny mix of Quentin Tarantino and David Fincher's unique styles combines to create something new, imperfect, and extremely exciting

Legendary filmmaker Stanley Kubrick died unexpectedly in his sleep in March 1999 at the age of 70, leaving behind a handful of unfinished projects that would never see the light of day. One of them, however, was eventually completed after Kubrick's close friend Steven Spielberg stepped in to direct A.I. Artificial Intelligence. The result is an oddly hypnotic melding of the two directors' distinct styles, making it one of the most unique films ever released. Artificial Intelligence isn't a perfect movie (it's nowhere near the top of either filmmaker's greatest hits), but there's something fascinating about seeing how their sensibilities overlap to create something totally new.

The story behind The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth isn't quite as dramatic, but the ultimate effect is similar. Nobody died. Quentin Tarantino just made the bizarre decision that his 10th film should be his last and that a sequel to Once Upon a Time in Hollywood wasn't going to cut it. So instead of trashing the film like he did with his last failed effort, Tarantino handed the script off to David Fincher. The result is another unusual melding of directorial styles that doesn't always work (it's definitely not the best either Fincher or Tarantino has to offer), but still manages to provide a uniquely fun time at the movies — and also on Netflix later this year.

The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth picks up eight years after Once Upon a Time... in Hollywood. Rick Dalton (Leonardo DiCaprio) is off in Australia starring in a popular new series, while his former stuntman Cliff (Brad Pitt) works a series of odd jobs in Los Angeles. One night he's serving drinks at a tiki bar with a mud wrestling ring​​​​​​​; another he manages the New Beverly Cinema (a one-screen theater owned by Tarantino himself IRL).

But Cliff's real profession has seemingly become professional fixer to the stars. In the film's opening scene, he helps retrieve a stolen Oscar for a director he's friends with, casually murdering one of the criminals and sending the other one back home crying to his mommy on a Greyhound bus. Throughout it all, Pitt remains cool and collected. He might just be the smoothest character Tarantino ever came up with, and that's saying a lot when the competition includes the Bible-quoting hitman Jules Winnfield (Samuel L. Jackson), the unflappable flight attendant Jackie Brown (Pam Grier), and pretty much every role played by Michael Madsen.

After that quick, scene-setting introduction, Tarantino's script gets to the meat of the story. Cliff receives an invitation to meet with TV star Charlie Peters (Scott Caan), which is odd because Charlie Peters famously does his own stunts. Turns out, the actor is in a serious jam with some Filipino gangsters who are threatening to murder his wife (Carla Gugino). Cliff reluctantly agrees to help, mostly because he's developed a crush on Charlie's beautiful assistant, Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki). Cliff Booth unfolds somewhat predictably from there. The gangsters pursue Charlie, Cliff pursues both the gangsters and Karen, and a series of misadventures and sidequests rise up along the way.

Tarantino also fills his script with the kind of meta-culture commentary we've come to expect, this time aimed squarely at the movie industry itself. The story overflows with films within films and made-up anecdotes from Hollywood history. At one point, the four main characters sit at a table and debate whether cinema even qualifies as an art form​​​​​​​, with Debicki delivering a scalding takedown​​​​​​​ of the entire industry that compares the choice between Star Wars and The Godfather to a Big Mac or a Whopper. Tarantino is playing the hits here, and I gleefully ate it up.

So what does Fincher bring to this unexpected fusion of styles? That's a tougher question to answer. Cliff Booth swaps the colorful comic-book pop of Tarantino's previous work for the same subtle gray filter that defines everything from Seven to The Social Network. Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross also continue their collaboration with Fincher, and their moody, noir-ish score further emphasizes that washed-out aesthetic​​​​​​​. The soundtrack is also full of '70s pop music, but if you're expecting a collection of Tarantino-level needledrops, think again​​​​​​​. Whoever picked the songs for this movie seriously phoned it in, with the most ambitious choice somehow being the AC/DC album title track "Dirty Deeds Done Dirt Cheap" playing over a demolition derby sequence. Another scene is punctuated with "It's a Shame" by The Spinners. It's almost as if someone typed in "1970s cool songs" on Spotify and let the algorithm do the work for them.

Gripes about the music aside, the world of 1970s Los Angeles is stunningly realized. The cars, the clothing, the street signs. It's all beautiful to behold, and Fincher's camera luxuriates in that aesthetic even more than Tarantino. Heck, even the vintage cans of beer and soda that Cliff guzzles down are fun to look at. At 2 hours and 20 minutes, Cliff Booth is by no means a breezy movie, but I could have spent even longer soaking in the world that Fincher and his team bring to life.

Cliff Booth doesn't exactly set up a sequel (the film's abrupt ending is arguably open to interpretation thanks to a bizarre mid-credits tag), but it's easy to imagine a world where we get to keep hanging out with Cliff for even longer. Like Benoit Blanc returning to solve each new Knives Out mystery, Brad Pitt's fixer could easily resurface a few years from now for another misadventure, ideally with Tarantino still writing the script. Fincher could return, too, but I'd be just as happy with another director taking the helm. What would a mashup between Tarantino and Richard Linklater or Greta Gerwig look like? I'm dying to find out. (Those are both huge longshots, but you get the idea.)

Even if we never see Cliff Booth again, I'm glad we have this weird little movie. It might not be perfect, but getting to spend a couple more hours in the world Tarantino created​​​​​​​ feels like a gift — especially when the director seems so hesitant to actually deliver his 10th and final film.

The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth will play in IMAX theaters only starting on Nov. 25, and releases on Netflix a month later on Dec. 23.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

I think Once Upon a Time in Hollywood is easily my least favorite Quentin Tarantino movie even more so than Deathproof. We get it you love 60s Hollywood, have a weird beef with the late Bruce Lee for some reason, and had the hots for Sharon Tate. The only saving grace of the movie is Leonardo DiCaprio performance as Rick Dalton. I can't say I'm all that eager to watch this because I was not a fan of the Cliff Booth character and that stupid ending where Quentin implies it would have stayed the 60s forever if only that darn Charles Manson and his followers didn't murder all those people.

#3486. ‘The Altruists’ Review: Netflix’s Slight Sam Bankman-Fried Series Tells a Strange, Crooked Love Story

Netflix’s “The Altruists,” the latest limited series about a modern-day tech scandal, posits a few sound-enough theories about what drives its featured fraudster to steal $8 billion of customers’ money. For instance, Sam Bankman-Fried (Anthony Boyle) grows up playing games but never actually grows up, so he struggles to perceive his cryptocurrency exchange, FTX, as anything beyond a game he’s meant to win. The unkempt, dead-eyed co-founder similarly has a hard time distinguishing between theoretical and actual consequences, so when a “mathematically optimal” strategy doesn’t pay out, all he sees is a smaller-than-expected number on the balance sheet — not a retirement account squandered or a college education lost. Related Stories Skydance to Combine Warner Bros. Television Group and Paramount Television Studios as One Big Studio ‘Elsinore’ Review: Andrew Scott’s Towering Performance as a Dying Actor Can’t Overcome AIDS-Movie Awards Bait Clichés

Arrested development and severe personalities are part and parcel for any tech founder story, so much so that, as a bleak sign of the times, they’re already being parodied. (In “The Audacity,” Billy Magnussen’s insecure, second-rate CEO loses his shit when a psych test shows he’s not on the spectrum.) On top of these familiar traits, “The Altruists” adds familiar language in the form of ear-piercing dog whistles — Sam speaks of of “moving fast” and “breaking things” one too many times — which make clear our antihero belongs among the villainous Silicon Valley set. He’s as much a product of the times as a very “special” boy.

Such echoes lend “The Altruists” a sense of “been there, broke that” amid a crowded Founders Fall. (Even if “The Social Reckoning” wasn’t for you, we all just rewatched “The Dropout,” no?) But creator and co-showrunner Graham Moore, alongside co-showrunner and executive producer Jacqueline Hoyt, center their scammer’s analysis around a fresh(ish) yet timeless vantage point: Sam is in love with Caroline Ellison (Julia Garner), and he has no idea how to express it. Their doomed romance sparks the creation and destruction of the third-largest digital currency exchange in the world (plus, you know, the subsequent prison sentences), as their inability to make sense of their emotions sullies their ethical ambitions for making billions (which were already pretty muddy).

It’s a shame, then, that their relationship proves as shallow as it is annoying. Wrapped in interminable, indicative nerd quirks — stutters and stammers, over-explanations and misplaced pride, regular references to Harry Potter, LARP, and math camp — Sam and Caroline’s grand romance isn’t sustainable enough entertainment to support an eight-hour story, nor is it explored with enough sincerity to break your heart (or expand your mind). Boyle and Garner’s performances are committed and their transformations convincing, but they’re in service of one theory about two people’s core deficiency that isn’t as revealing or rewarding as it needs to be.

Sam and Caroline’s meet-cute takes place — where else — at work. In 2016, Sam is an ambitious go-getter on Wall Street. His custom algorithms have earned attention from the higher-ups after successfully predicting the election results and then trading off those results to the tune of $150 million in profit. …but then those same algorithms doubled down and ended up losing twice what they initially made. So, as punishment, Sam is sent to interview interns, where he meets and bonds with a fellow trader.

During an introductory quiz, Caroline determines there’s no prize for second place, which means it’s the same as last place, so the “mathematically optimal strategy is to go all-in every time.” It’s the same strategy Sam used to win when he was an intern, and although Caroline goes bust, she’s hits big with Sam. His parents taught at Stanford, so he went to MIT to get away from them. Her parents taught at MIT, so she went to Stanford. They both were expected to be child math prodigies, but neither “prodigied.” Her ultimate goal is to solve the global water crisis. His is goal is equally altruistic, if much more vague.

“Look, I know I haven’t done it yet,” Sam says to Caroline. “Little things here and there, sure, but the big thing? I’m a little behind schedule. But I’m going to do it.”

His conviction wins her over — especially when they meet again, by chance, at a meeting for Effective Altruists — and soon enough they’re misreading flirtations and fumbling through his first sexual encounter. As they leave Wall Street behind to focus on “the big thing,” “The Altruists” jumps ahead to its second predominant timeline: Where their initial courtship and company start-ups take place in “Part 1: Rise,” even more screentime is dedicated to “Part II: Fall,” which picks up in 2022 when evidence of their theft starts to leak amid a massive party in the Bahamas.

The multiple-timeline structure ostensibly juxtaposes past promises from present betrayals, but it’s hardly necessary to get the point across (“how things have changed” doesn’t hit as hard when the characters look the same) and actively harmful to the supporting cast. Using “Rise” as the A-plot and “Fall” as the B-plot keeps Sam and Caroline in the center of things, which proves exhausting when they keep repeating themselves and strands everyone else in one-note (or sometimes no-note) archetypes who mainly exist to yell at the two leads.

Sam Trabucco (Alex Lawther) is the mirror version of Sam Bankman-Fried, a sweet, self-assured kid who actually believes in what FTX is doing, until the hard truth of what they’ve actually done sends him fleeing to the open seas. (SBF stays put, living in his delusion of innocence.) Nishad Singh (Karan Soni) is another mirror, first as a friend from the neighborhood who bonded with Mr. Bankman (Paul Reiser) and Mrs. Fried (Robin Weigert) in a way Sam never could, and later as a fellow sufferer of unrequited love for a co-worker, only his heart is pure where Sam’s is tainted.

Eight hours of the immoral, motormouthed, future-then-former billionaire is a lot to tolerate, especially when his greatest obstacle is one we know he’ll never overcome: Sam and Caroline may be stupidly brilliant with numbers, but they’re just plain stupid when it comes to emotions. “I don’t think you can smart your way out of feelings,” Sam is told when our central couple first starts dating — but that doesn’t stop them from trying. Start to finish, Sam never says the words, “I love you,” despite each episode pivoting around a noxious will-they-or-won’t-they relationship that ebbs and flows between a full-on, loud-and-proud romance and a business partnership manufactured to keep them together when logic alone could not.

Tolerance may vary, but after a few hours, “The Altruists” is too cutesy, too aware of its own cuteness, and ultimately too dedicated to the wrong questions: What went wrong with FTX has been explained again and again, and the series doesn’t pass up its chance to play the hits. (It’s “inspired by” a series of New York Magazine articles.) But “The Altruists” has the chance to consider what went wrong with Sam and Caroline’s souls, and it doesn’t dig deep enough to expose anything more than emptiness.

At its best, “The Altruists” is a whirlwind depiction of love not as a beautiful, life-saving devotion, but as an illogical and immoral excuse to wreak havoc. (Think of it as the most unlikely spinoff to “The Last of Us.”) Sam and Caroline use each other to justify unscrupulous (and illegal) actions that stack up until they’re trapped by the sheer scope of their misjudgment. But at least they’re trapped together. It’s a love story and an anti-love story at once; the audience sees the latter and the subjects convince themselves it’s the former.

That’s fascinating territory to explore, thematically and internally, but Moore and Hoyt’s series tells you what it’s about — explicitly, repeatedly, unmistakably — and then reiterates that statement over and over as the situations escalate. Ultimately, it gets caught in the same quandary as its subjects: The relationship’s pointed lack of evolution proves more redundant than revelatory, so when it comes to emotional enlightenment, “The Altruists” is out of its depth.

“The Altruists” premieres Thursday, November 19 on Netflix. All eight episodes will be released at once.

#3485. The Rings Of Power Season 3's Incest Storyline Is A Big Change From The Books – And It Could Have Been Much Worse

One does not simply walk into spoilers. This article discusses major plot details up to "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" Season 3, Episode 6.

When it comes to a story as sprawling and complex as "The Lord of the Rings," not all adaptation changes are made equally. Throughout three seasons of "The Rings of Power," showrunners J.D. Payne and Patrick McKay have given us plenty to choose from. Some, like the arrival of Gandalf (Daniel Weyman), make perfect sense — although technically he's not meant to be involved in the action until centuries later in the timeline, you can understand why the series' creatives would want to speed things up a bit. Others, like the decision to keep Galadriel (Morfydd Clark) and her husband Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower) apart for so long, took longer to come into focus.

While many of the headlines will center on the deception of Charlie Vickers' Sauron and his breakthrough in figuring out how to forge the One Ring, an under-the-radar twist revealed itself all the way in the west on the island kingdom of Númenor. For several episodes, we've watched rivals and royal cousins Pharazôn (Trystan Gravelle) and Míriel (Cynthia Addai-Robinson) come closer and closer to outright conflict over the throne. How they resolve this may seem to line up with author J.R.R. Tolkien's original telling, but the circumstances vary considerably.

Now we know why the Prime Video series changed things up. In the latest episode, their attempts to negotiate and avoid bloody civil war reach an impasse ... until Pharazôn finds an unexpected solution. Actually, make that a proposal. Yes, this is the moment "The Rings of Power" takes a page out of the "House of the Dragon" playbook. And it could've been much worse.

"The Lord of the Rings" may have a reputation as cozy, comforting fantasy with its plucky Hobbits and kindly old wizards, but don't look past the abject darkness at the heart of the story. J.R.R. Tolkien never shied away from the shortcomings of individuals throughout his tales — in fact, as a Catholic, he emphasized them. But all it takes is a cursory look at the lore and mythology preceding his most famous novels to realize just how much Middle-earth has in common with the likes of Westeros in "Game of Thrones."

Don't believe us? Look no further than how "The Rings of Power" begins to resolve one of its biggest storylines in Season 3. After several episodes of Númenor coming perilously close to tearing itself apart, we're left on an unsettling cliffhanger. The usurper Pharazôn suggests that he and Míriel repair this rift through an incestuous political marriage. It's clear from the look on Míriel's face that this is a measure of last resort, but everything about her arc thus far implies that she'll end up putting the greater good of the kingdom over her own desires (which, remember, are more romantically inclined towards Lloyd Owen's noble Elendil).

Still, this is far tamer than how Tolkien originally tells it. While the appendices found at the end of "The Return of the King" are light on details, other sources (like "The Silmarillion") explain how Pharazôn looked enviously upon the rightful heir Míriel, forced his cousin into marriage against her will and against all the laws of the land, and took power. Compared to this, "The Rings of Power" gives Míriel far more agency.

Those who know their J.R.R. Tolkien ought to be well familiar with where "The Rings of Power" is going next. (For those who don't, be advised this next section dives into major potential spoilers.) With only two episodes to go in Season 3 and the bulk of it likely taking place on the mainland, the Númenor plot will soon need to resolve itself. Míriel must still actually agree to Pharazôn's terms and avoid a costly battle, thus allowing their combined forces to look outwards and send their armada to assist the beleaguered Elves attempting to resist against Sauron.

But it's what comes next, almost certain to unfold in Season 4, that concerns us the most. With their power soon to be consolidated in an uneasy alliance, Míriel and Pharazôn will eventually have to contend with that pesky Dark Lord. According to the various texts, this is the pivotal inflection point that puts us on a path towards the inevitable Fall of Númenor. According to Tolkien's original writings, Númenor's entrance into the war has disastrous consequences. Granted, their fearsome army quickly overwhelms Sauron's own and leads to him being taken back to the island as a prisoner, but that's where all the troubles begin. Eventually, Sauron worms his way into Pharazôn's ear and convinces him to set his sights on the Valar themselves — a desperate gambit to stave off death among Mortal Men and seize the eternal life that's been denied them.

None of this ends well for Númenor, but we're getting ahead of ourselves. The final two episodes of "The Rings of Power" Season 3 stream November 25, 2026, on Prime Video.

#3484. The Unexpected History of 'Black Friday'

Since the 1950s, Black Friday—once simply known as "the day after Thanksgiving"—has grown into a quasi-holiday in the United States marked by steep discounts, ceaseless shopping, and occasional violence. But more recently, Black Friday has also metastasized. It's not a day anymore. It's a week, a month, a veritable state of mind. (Speaking of which, check out Lifehacker's Black Friday coverage. We got all the deals, baby!)

While pre-dawn trips to the mall are waning as online shopping grows, in-person shopping on Black Friday is still a big deal in the U.S.—it’s estimated that around 80 million Americans visited a brick-and-mortar store on Black Friday in 2025. But how did Black Friday come about, and what does it all mean?

“Black Friday” in the United States originally referred to the start of the Panic of 1869, when the collapse of the price of gold devastated the national economy. “Black Friday” as a description of the day after Thanksgiving dates back to 1951; the term first appeared in the journal Factory Management and Maintenance, where it referred to the number of employees who skipped work on the day after Thanksgiving. Around the same time, the police in Philadelphia and Rochester started informally using “Black Friday” to describe the traffic and crowds that appeared in their cities as shoppers hit the stores on the day after Thanksgiving. The phrase gradually caught on. It was picked up by national press in 1975 when the New York Times used "Black Friday" specifically to describe the day after Thanksgiving and the shopping and sales it brings.

But even before it had a name, Black Friday was a thing. The day after Thanksgiving has been known by merchants as the start of the shopping season since the late 1800s. By the early 20th century, retailers sponsored Thanksgiving Day parades that traditionally ended with an appearance by Santa Claus, as if to say, “Now it’s time to shop for Christmas.” By unspoken agreement among retailers, Christmas-themed advertisements rarely appeared before Thanksgiving in our grandparents’ day. This informal bargain obviously no longer applies.

Referring to a day as “black” traditionally denotes a period of calamity or tragedy, leading some to suggest different names for the day. In the early 1960s, Philadelphia merchants suggested “Big Friday,” a name which did not catch on, leaving retailers with the weak explanation that the “black” in Black Friday refers to the black ink denoting profits in a ledger. Oft-repeated lore suggests that retailers are "in the red" all year, and only start making an annual profit at the end of the year, but big retail chains generally make money all year long.

A more modern issue with the name is that Black Friday sales now last for days or even weeks, beginning in early to mid-November and bleeding over into the following Saturday, Sunday, “Cyber Monday,” Tuesday, and beyond, leading people to say things like, “Do you want to go Black Friday shopping this Sunday?” So far, alternative names like “Five-Day Frenzy” and “The day I get to trample someone to save $8 on a Nespresso” haven’t caught on. But here’s hoping.

Beginning around 2010, an insatiable thirst for profits led many retailers to push the start of Black Friday shopping to Thursday (aka Thanksgiving Day). Kmart opened Thanksgiving morning. Toys R Us opened that night. By 2011, Walmart was opening its doors at 10 p.m. on Thursday. The trend led to widespread backlash, with many Americans appalled that employees were forced to work on Thanksgiving or angry that consumerism was encroaching upon a holiday meant to celebrate colonialism. By 2021, most major retailers had relented and elected to remain closed on Thanksgiving.

The term “Cyber Monday” describes the boost in online retail sales on the Monday after Thanksgiving, sparked by workers returning to the office and getting right to online shopping. The term first appeared on Nov. 28, 2005, in a Shop.org press release entitled “'Cyber Monday’ Quickly Becoming One of the Biggest Online Shopping Days of the Year," which may be the most influential press release ever written. Since its early 2000s birth, Cyber Monday has become the biggest online shopping day of the year. Americans spent $14.25 billion online on Cyber Monday 2025, according to Adobe Analytics. So is Cyber Monday bigger than Black Friday? Retailers really don't care: Analysts now tend to mash everything into the category of "Black Friday–Cyber Monday" (or even "Cyber Week").

If all this naked consumerism makes you a little squeamish, you're not alone. Anti-consumerists have named the day after Thanksgiving “Buy Nothing Day,” which you can celebrate by doing charity work, cutting up your credit cards, or simply not purchasing anything. Pioneered by artist Ted Dave and popularized by Adbusters magazine, the first Buy Nothing Day was celebrated in Canada in 1992.

It’s hard to measure the success of the alternative holiday. Both online and brick-and-mortar retail sales have increased sharply since 1992, suggesting Buy Nothing Day’s effect is negligible. On the other hand, maybe big retailers are losing millions because someone on Bluesky reminded you not to shop. Sure.

Depending on how you measure it, Black Friday has resulted in between one and 17 deaths. Jdimytai Damour is the only person killed directly due to a Black Friday sale: The 34-year-old worker was trampled to death by a surging crowd at a Long Island Walmart on Black Friday in 2008. If you include car accidents, shootings, retail worker suicides, and fatal heart attacks, Black Friday’s death toll balloons to 17, with 128 reported injuries.

Black Friday violence has even inspired a horror flick: Eli Roth's 2023 holiday-themed slasher Thanksgiving opens with a hilariously brutal Black Friday riot at a big box store, setting off a chain of events that involve a lot of people being murdered by a dude in a Pilgrim mask.

I mean, yeah, of course. Critics of Black Friday point out that there are arguably better times to buy a new TV (like the week before the Super Bowl), not to mention plenty of other goods. Savings from Black Friday shopping are often illusory—big-ticket “doorbuster” items generally sell out quickly, leaving behind goods that are, by and large, priced the same as they would be at any other time of year. Some retailers even mark up products ahead of Black Friday so the discounts look bigger. If you're buying online, your browser history, location, and cart contents can tweak the prices you see on Black Friday, as they can on any other day.

Yet despite protest holidays, the unpleasantness of shopping when stores are overcrowded, and the frustration of hunting for bargains that often aren't that great to begin with, Black Friday stubbornly remains an unofficial holiday, celebrated by over 100 million Americans in one way or another. What that says about our country's relationship with capitalism is unclear, but personally, I’m going to continue my own day-after-Thanksgiving tradition of eating pie for breakfast and thinking about going for a walk, but then watching The Quick and the Dead instead. I'm not protesting anything; I just don't need the hassle.

#3481. Disney Plus Reveals Official Cast for Zombie Apocalypse Reboot of Classic Comic

Say goodbye to Riverdale and hello to Afterlife with Archie

It's been a little over three years since Riverdale, the CW's loose adaptation of the Archie Comics characters, aired its final episode. Now Disney is gearing up to bring audiences back to the town of Riverdale, but it will be in a wildly different way. As announced this July, Disney Plus is set to release an adaptation of the horror comic Afterlife with Archie next year. Now we know who will play Archie, Betty, Veronica, and more.

As reported by Deadline, executive producer Roberto Aguirre-Sacasa has begun casting the series. Aguirre-Sacasa is the chief creative officer of Archie Comics and wrote the original Afterlife with Archie comic, in addition to developing Riverdale. Vasco Faria will play Archie Andrews​​​​​​​, Aliyah Mastin (Paradise) will play Veronica Lodge, Sarah Abbott (The Body) will portray Betty Cooper, Angel Rivera will play Jughead Jones, and Sabrina Spellman will be played by Chloe Avakian.

While it didn't make sense for the cast of Riverdale to return, it will be hard to move on from​​​​​​​ that show's iconic and over-the-top takes on the classic characters. Afterlife with Archie will give the new cast plenty of opportunity to make the characters their own​​​​​​​, though, as the story sees the residents of Riverdale dealing with a zombie apocalypse​​​​​​​ caused by Sabrina casting a spell to revive Jughead's dog. The show is slated to premiere on Halloween 2027.

The original Afterlife with Archie​​​​​​​ comic was written by Aguirre-Sacasa with art by Francesco Francavilla. The comic first released in 2013 and ran for ten issues. The series, however, did not continue beyond those ten issues.​​​​​​​ According to Aguirre-Sacasa, that doesn't mean the comic has been canceled.

In fact,​​​​​​​ when Disney initially announced it had ordered an adaptation of the series, Aguirre-Sacasa revealed he had returned to work on the comic as well. He announced this about a year ago​​​​​​​ and there have been few updates since​​​​​​​. Reportedly,​​​​​​​ issues 11 and 12 have been written and issue 13 was being plotted​​​​​​​,with Francavilla resuming writing duties. Perhaps the comic will return​​​​​​​ ahead of the show's premiere next year.

#3479. Friday The 13th (2027) Movie Cast, Title And Everything We Know So Far

For 17 years, sex-crazed teenagers with a penchant for getting high and/or drunk have had a veritable field day. Jason Voorhees, horror's deadliest and most dedicated moralist has been nowhere to be seen. It was starting to look like the only thing that could vanquish Jason for good was a protracted lawsuit, but now, Horror, Inc., which controls the rights to the machete-wielding killer, has moved forward with a new installment titled "Jason." Barring more legal shenanigans, he's set to slay anew on August 13, 2027.

Horror, Inc., Jason Universe, and Cineverse announced the news in a press release, which includes the announcement of the new film's final girl, Natalie Alyn Lind as Lauren. You might know her from "Dutton Ranch" or the X-Men television series "The Gifted." I find it kinda curious that they're revealing the final girl so far ahead of time. It's typically not hard to identify who's going to be the last girl standing, but there have been some reasonably decent fake-outs in previous movies (I thought Barbara Howard's virginal Sara in "Friday the 13th: The Final Chapter" had a shot at surviving the night). I dunno, maybe they're planning to pull the rug out from under us and kill Lind off early.

The other major announcement is that stunt coordinator Schuyler White will don the hockey mask as Jason Voorhees. Horror, Inc.'s "franchise steward" Robbie Barsamian believes White has the build and presence to be the "most intimidating" Jason ever. Per Barsamian, "[White] approached this theatrical feature like the role of a lifetime, packing 30 pounds of solid muscle onto his 6'5″ frame and studying the iconic Jasons who came before him so that he feels like an unstoppable force of nature." We'll see about that.

"Jason" wrapped production today after a fairly brief shoot that started in October. It's directed by Steve Miner, who helmed "Friday the 13th Part II" and "Friday the 13th Part III" (in which Jason first slipped on the mask, pictured in the images above). In a recent interview with The Wrap, Barsamian gave fans an idea of what to expect. "This is the scariest and most brutal movie we've ever made," he said. Okay then.

He went on to say, "We made sure to hold onto all the core elements that make Jason and 'Friday the 13th' what it is. Innovative kills, practical effects, scares and that classic slasher energy, but we really raised the bar across the board. The kills in this film are easily the most creative, brutal, bloody and visceral we've ever done."

As for the fresh meat, the probable victims include Matt Corney ("High School Musical: The Musical: The Series") as Asher, Lilia Buckingham ("Hocus Pocus 2") as Madison, John Owen Lowe ("Unstable") as Jake, Summer Madison ("The Summer I Turned Pretty") as Emily, Selena Turner ("Will Trent") as Olive, Matthew Keoni Sato ("High School Musical: The Musical: The Series") as Lucas, Brook Sill ("Stranger Things") as Zoe, Guillermo Diaz ("Scandal") as Rick, Johnell Young ("Wu-Tang: An American Saga") as Frank, Sencere M. Brown ("Homage") as Chase, and Bryan Gael Guzman ("Nickel Boys") as Dylan.

When it comes to raising the bar on kills, I can't help but wonder if they'll try to measure up to the gloriously grotesque mayhem unleashed by Johnny in "In a Violent Nature." Horror fans have become accustomed to new levels of brutality. We'll see if the old pro Miner can recapture the slasher magic.

#3478. Should the Oscars Keep Nominating Diane Warren?

As a third year in a row winning at the Hollywood Music in Media Awards primes songwriter Diane Warren for her 18th Best Original Song Oscar nomination, IndieWire Editor at Large Anne Thompson and Awards Editor Marcus Jones debate whether or not that recognition is still warranted.

Anne Thompson: For Hollywood outsiders, there’s an unsolved mystery every year at the Oscars. Why does songwriter Diane Warren keep getting nominated for movies nobody has ever heard of? Most Best Original Song nominees come from popular movies that many Music Branch voters have seen. But every year Diane Warren gets in there. She’s been nominated 17 times and never won. And even though the Academy presented her with an honorary Oscar in 2022, the Music Branch keeps nominating her anyway, thus taking her slot away from some other deserving songwriter. Why? Related Stories Where Are the Women? Zero Female Directors on Blumhouse Atomic’s Theatrical Slate for 2027 ‘Bedford Park’ Trailer: Sundance Winner Stars Moon Choi, Who Falls for the Other Driver in Her Mother’s Car Accident

Marcus Jones: Well, I would hardly say every Best Original Song nominee comes from a popular film. Did you see “Viva Verdi!” last year? And who is this other deserving songwriter you speak of? Let’s get into the crux of your arguments.

Anne Thompson: It’s politics, stupid. “She’s ruthless,” one Music Branch member told me. In other words, she campaigns hard for her slot every year. At the Middleburg Film Festival this fall, she flagged down people she knew in the hallways to show them her latest song on her mobile phone, a soaring duet between Jennifer Hudson and tenor Andrea Bocelli for the upcoming Al Pacino movie “Maserati: The Brothers,” which no one has seen. She even had a documentary made about her, “Relentless,” referring not only to how people in Hollywood describe her, but also to her bracelet inscribed “relentless as fuck.” The well-reviewed movie sells her brand perfectly: Its tagline is “Hitmaker. Legend. Pain in the ass.” You have to hand it to her: She’s a self-promotional marketing whiz. And by the way, she’s fun to hang out with, no question.

Marcus Jones: While that behavior at Middleburg that you described was quite forward, there is a positive spin on her relentless campaigning. At a time when the number of films nominated each year seems to be shrinking, and awards campaigns are getting more expensive, Warren’s one-woman awards run has turned truly independent films into Oscar nominees. Regardless of how you feel about the film or the song, it is truly inspiring to see films, often with no major studio backing, find a way into the conversation. Campaigning works!

Anne Thompson: Her fellow Music Branch members, especially in L.A., know her well. She’s been in the business for over four decades. She’s friends with most of them and invites them to her home every winter for a lavish holiday party.

Marcus Jones: Correct, she has had a head start with all these people, but this kind of indirect campaigning is not uncommon. For example, the president of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences was a guest at the biggest celebrity wedding of the year, the bride being another current Best Original Song contender.

Anne Thompson: I would call it direct campaigning. The Music Branch voters identify with Warren. Many of the members are on the senior side of their careers. They got into the Academy for music they wrote decades ago, like Warren. She writes melodic tunes that they like.

Marcus Jones: That is something that I feel is lost in the conversation around her nominations. Take away all 17 songs she’s been nominated for, and she is still one of the most accomplished songwriters of all time. This is a woman who wrote both Toni Braxton’s “Un-Break My Heart” and Cher’s “If I Could Turn Back Time” — definitive songs for those artists. As a songwriter, even if you reach the upper echelon of having a chart-topping run, that often lasts a decade at best. Warren has found a lane that has garnered her recognition from her community year after year, over four decades into her career.

Anne Thompson: But songs she wrote four decades ago should have nothing to do with how well her most recent song serves her current movie. She manages to get a few songs into movies every year and submits them. Winning a competitive Oscar is her goal in life! Her fellow members admire her pluck, tenacity, and drive. And there’s a question of whether the Music Branch watches the movies at all — most look and listen to video clips. Let’s be honest. The Music Branch is often swayed by concerns other than what is the best song in a movie, like, who is a major pop star they’d like to see perform on the Oscar telecast.

Marcus Jones: I personally find that to be one of the biggest misconceptions about the Music Branch. If they were actually swayed by who they think the most people would want to see on the telecast, then stadium acts like Taylor Swift, Ed Sheeran, and Miley Cyrus — who have all made several attempts at a Best Original Song nomination — would have gotten one by now. Bias is absolutely a factor in who gets nominated, but the members are also very discerning about how the song is used in the movie. The Best Original Song category was meant to honor music that holds significance to the film. Warren tends to be more mindful than many other musicians on that front. Even when producing music videos for her contenders, it’s never just about whether the song is good, but how much it is in conversation with the film it was written for. Her songs never feel tacked onto a project.

Anne Thompson: Another reason the Music Branch votes for her: Many of them owe her. “She got me into the Academy,” one voter said. According to one music publicist, she sponsors two Academy applicants a year. Those favors add up.

Marcus Jones: Hard to argue with that. Notable, too, that she keeps all her own publishing rights, which any songwriter will tell you is an incredible (and incredibly lucrative) feat. Though that likely creates a challenge for her when it comes to working with bigger studios. Many of those have record labels that are sister companies. We’re at a time where songwriters are often asked to give artists a cut of the publishing, to project the idea that they write all their own songs.

Anne Thompson: What bothers me most is the many slots that could have gone to someone else. Warren is successful and respected by her peers. She is being selfish and greedy. She doesn’t need a second Oscar. Let another worthy songwriter have a shot.

Marcus Jones: If you were successful enough in your discipline to keep getting nominated, why would you ever stop trying to win? No one accused composer Randy Newman or cinematographer Roger Deakins of taking the nomination slot of this phantom contender who is supposedly more deserving, and both were nominated over a dozen times before they won their first Oscar. The Best Sound category alone has a history of contenders breaking the record for most nominations with no wins. There wasn’t press telling re-recording mixer Kevin O’Connell to give up and get out of the way after 20 tries. One can dislike her music and her methods, but writing original songs for films is a task Warren takes very seriously. At this point, she sets the bar that songwriters must clear to have a chance at winning, and few do.

#3476. 42 Years Later, The Terminator's Most Famous Line Is Still The Greatest Sci-Fi Movie Quote

"The Terminator" bowed in 1984 but was so ahead of its time it could easily debut today and be just as, if not more relevant. The film's encapsulation of society's collective fear of a technological future gave what would have otherwise been a sci-fi slasher B-movie real depth. Paired with James Cameron's still-developing yet impressive filmmaking skills, honed over years spent toiling for Roger Corman's New World Pictures and a particularly unfortunate experience on 1982's "Piranha II: The Spawning," that remarkable prescience made the film an instant classic that also happened to give its star, Arnold Schwarzenegger, his most memorable catchphrase.

Long before 2019's "Terminator: Dark Fate" made Schwarzenegger give up on the franchise altogether, Cameron's original masterpiece combined elements of the burgeoning slasher genre with sci-fi and action spectacle to create a truly original moviegoing experience (even if the insatiably litigious Harlan Ellison claimed "The Terminator" was all his idea). The fact that any movie gets produced is a marvel in its own way, but "The Terminator" was a real miracle, wrought by the sheer will of its director and his producing partner Gale Anne Hurd to actually get the film made. Their persistence paid off. What could have easily been an overlooked low-budget sci-fi actioner became a modest sensation, making $78.4 million on a $6.4 million budget and launching Cameron's career.

Clearly, the writer/director had tapped into something larger with his story of a murderous cyborg sent back through time to kill the woman who would birth the leader of the human resistance. Audiences were enraptured and 42 years later the movie remains just as chillingly pertinent and wildly entertaining as it was in the mid-'80s. As such, Arnie's most famous line arguably remains the greatest sci-fi quote of all time.

Arnold Schwarzenegger initially had no interest in "The Terminator, which considering this film (alongside his lead performance in 1982's "Conan the Barbarian") turned him into a movie star is hard to believe. Similarly, the Austrian Oak was reluctant to deliver what has since become the movie's most memorable line. Thankfully, James Cameron won him over.

The scene in question sees Arnie's Terminator arrive at a police station in search of Linda Hamilton's Sarah Connor. There, he's told by the officer on duty to take a seat and wait. Big mistake. Presumably, this unstoppable killer robot could have just punched his way through the glass facade between him and the officer before rampaging through the station to find his target. But that's no fun. Instead, Cameron — who would later jump a semi-truck into a Los Angeles viaduct in "Terminator 2: Judgment Day" — decided to have Arnie's robot ram a sedan through the doors of the station and into the reception desk, pinning the officer to the wall. Before he does so, however, the Terminator says the line.

After the officer tells him to take a seat, Schwarzenegger calmly takes a look around, leans in and says three words: "I'll be back." Of course, he's referring to the fact he'll soon ram the policeman between a wall and a car. But like the movie in which they're spoken, the words proved to be oddly prophetic. The Terminator did return, multiple times. Only the aforementioned "T2" lived up to the original, but the simple phrase, "I'll be back," almost came to represent the way in which "The Terminator" and its sequel remain perennially relevant as we hurtle towards the AI-driven garbage future that awaits.

"That Terminator is out there. It can't be bargained with. It can't be reasoned with. It doesn't feel pity, or remorse, or fear. And it absolutely will not stop, ever, until you are dead!"

"You still don't get it, do you? He'll find her! That's what he does! That's all he does! You can't stop him! He'll wade through you, reach down her throat, and pull her f****** heart out!"

"Your son gave me a message to give to you. He made me memorize it. 'Thank you, Sarah, for your courage through the dark years. I can't help you with what you must soon face except to say that the future is not set. You must be stronger than you imagine you can be. You must survive or I will never exist.' That's all."

#3474. How to play pool in GTA 6

To play pool in Grand Theft Auto 6, you must find a table and know the rules. You'll likely play your first game of pool during the "Coming Home" mission at the Rusty Anchor, but the game assumes some familiarity with the game of pool. Don't worry; playing pool (and winning!) is easy once you get the hang of it.

Here's where and how to play pool in GTA 6.

Pool isn't listed as an activity on the map legend, but if a location contains a pool table, you will see a small 8-ball icon when you hover over it on the map. To find new pool tables, you'd best look for bars, clubs, and gyms. One pool table isn't different from another, but it can be hard to find one with a challenger present. If you're up for some competition, you'd best go to the pool table at The Rusty Anchor.

Playing pool in GTA 6 doesn't yield much money, but it will boost your focus by a few percent per game.

While you can practice solo anytime you want, if there's an opponent waiting at the pool table, you can accept their challenge (which requires cash). Don't expect to walk away rich; the prize pot is usually no more than $20. Alternatively, you can invite your partner to play pool with you, which will improve your relationship.

To get started, pick up a cue — it's usually on the wall, near the pool table. Now, take your break shot; hold L2/LT to aim, then either use the left trigger to manually hit the white cue ball (pull it back, then move forward) or hold and release R2/RT. For now, aim forward in a straight line and hit the cue ball with enough power to scatter the rest of the balls.

From this point onward, you and your opponent will take turns trying to push the colored balls into the six holes on the edges of the table, via the cue ball. Initially, you and your opponent are free to score with any type of ball except the black 8-ball — if you pocket it, you'll lose the game. Beware that the first person to pocket a ball is assigned that type of ball. So, if you score first by pocketing a striped ball, you'll have to pocket every other striped ball to win the game. Your opponent, in that case, must pocket every solid ball.

If you hit no balls, your opponent's balls, or the 8-ball first, your opponent can place the cue ball in a better spot at the start of their next turn. If you successfully pocket a ball from your own group, you get an extra shot. Once you've pocketed every ball within your group, you only need to pocket the 8-ball to win the game. It's important to note that you do not need to call which pocket you'll hit the 8-ball into to win.

While GTA 6's version of pool is very realistic, there are still a few exploits to help you win every game.

#3473. The Rings Of Power Season 3 Is Loosely Remaking A Familiar Lord Of The Rings Storyline

Spoilers are never late, nor are they early, but arrive precisely when they mean to. This article discusses major plot details from "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" Season 3 Episodes 5-6.

Ages may pass, tyrants come and go, but some things in Middle-earth never change. As we reach the endgame of "The Rings of Power" Season 3, the Prime Video series is approaching the halfway point of its five-season plan. Although this takes place thousands of years before the events of "The Lord of the Rings," this inevitably means that Middle-earth is beginning to look much like the version we remember from Peter Jackson's spiritually-related (though canonically separate) films.

The looming threat of Charlie Vickers' Sauron is the most obvious link between the Second and Third Ages of J.R.R. Tolkien's fantasy epic, of course, but the similarities extend far beyond the self-styled Lord of the Rings. The various peoples of the land still profoundly distrust each other despite their common enemy, Ringwraiths are on the prowl, and everything's building to the forging of the One Ring to rule them all. But don't look past one of the most surprising developments of all: the brewing rivalry between Daniel Weyman's Gandalf and the so-called Dark Wizard Pallando (Ciarán Hinds).

In Episode 3, we learned that Gandalf's purpose was to save Pallando rather than defeat him, but our Grey wizard quickly finds this easier said than done. Pallando the Blue has found himself backed into a corner, caught between a Nazgnagôl and a Dark Lord. And no matter how much Gandalf urges him to join their power together and unite against their foe, the Dark Wizard's actions in Episode 5 give us a wizard-on-wizard fight that feels like a remake of Gandalf's struggles with Saruman centuries later.

As a certain "Star Wars" director once so memorably put it, "It's like poetry, sort of. They rhyme." Obviously, George Lucas was trying to verbalize the idea of mythology and lore echoing through the ages — humans love ourselves some cyclical storytelling, after all. "The Lord of the Rings" is no different. In this case, "The Rings of Power" has the added challenge of having to live in the shadow of an all-timer trilogy and contend with an audience that has come to view those movies as the definitive version of this story.

Well, if you can't beat 'em, join 'em. Showrunners J.D. Payne and Patrick McKay opted for a trip down memory lane with Gandalf and Pallando's long-awaited reunion after Season 2. Burdened with the glorious purpose of redeeming his fellow wizard (as handed down by the Secret Fire), Gandalf tries to reason with the Dark Wizard ... before things ultimately turn violent. Between Pallando's entreaties that they must "kneel" to Sauron and the subsequent duel with their magical staffs, it's all very reminiscent of a similar moment in "The Fellowship of the Ring." While visiting his "old friend," Gandalf realizes to his horror that the great wizard Saruman (Christopher Lee) is now in thrall to Sauron and now urges Gandalf to "join" him.

From the dialogue to the fight choreography to Bear McCreary's score, this sequence clearly attempts to evoke the Saruman/Gandalf dynamic for viewers. But, rather than serve as a mere reference for the sake of it, this actually helps make this battle more meaningful. Down the line, hundreds and hundreds of years in the future, we can imagine an older and wiser Gandalf remembering this encounter with Pallando when he visits Saruman.

What's a magical wizard's duel or two between very old friends? As Gandalf learns early on in "The Rings of Power" Season 3, the all-powerful godlike being known as Eru Ilúvatar sent five wizards (known as Istari) to Middle-earth. In the official canon laid down by J.R.R. Tolkien, this occurred early in the Third Age — the same time period that the events of "The Lord of the Rings" take place in — as a way to bring aid during Sauron's latest return. In "The Rings of Power," this has been moved up to the Second Age and it's easy to see why. As a result, the creative team can now use this meeting between Gandalf and Pallando (which doesn't take place in any of Tolkien's texts) to reflect and echo his later experience with Saruman.

It's a neat, ironic twist that this happens to involve a Dark Wizard whom many fans once thought might be Saruman himself. Instead, Episode 5 uses Pallando the Blue as a parallel to Saruman the White's eerily similar fall into darkness. Since this subplot is entirely missing from Episode 6, we'll have to wait and see how Episode 7 and the finale wrap things up — whether Gandalf proves successful in his mission to win Pallando back from the clutches of evil, or if Pallando's mysterious vision from the Secret Fire proves true and his doom really does come at the hands of "a ring-bearer" as he foresaw.

Either way, this lends all sorts of weight to Gandalf's later struggle with Saruman. Seeing one wizarding friend turn to the dark side is bad enough, but reliving it all over again? That's some serious trauma.

Loam Entertainment has started production this month on “Epic Zombie Christmas,” the follow-up to their summer camp film, “Bad Counselors.” Descried as a “heartfelt comedy,” the family film will focus on an unexpected intergenerational connection between teen filmmakers and the eccentric senior citizen stars of their Christmas zombie movie. Despite the generational delta, the group bonds over their emotional, creative journey that eventually bonds them.

Nathan Frankowski (“Te Ata”) directs from a script written by Frankowski and Dexter Masland (“Bad Counselors”). The film’s teen stars include Alex J. Montero (“Law & Order: SVU”), Carson Bolde (“Godzilla”), Chandni Shah (“Jailed Bird”), Indi Star (“Charmers”), and Jacob Buster (“Ballers”). #3470. GTA 6 Players Should Change This One Setting Before Anything Else

GTA 6 includes some key settings that make it move a bit quicker

Now that Grand Theft Auto 6 is out, players are discovering that Rockstar Games' latest feels more like Red Dead Redemption 2 than GTA 5. Rockstar Games builds on the work it did in its open-world western and applies it to the context of a modern city. That’s a big part of why it's so successful, but that might make some players nervous. While GTA 6 moves at a quicker pace, movement can still feel a little slower than you might expect​​​​​​​.

If you’re in that boat, don't worry: GTA 6 includes a few important settings that you can toggle on to speed up the pace.

First, you have to understand the nuances of movement in GTA 6. Jason and Lucia have three movement states: walk, jog, and run. By default, they’ll trot at a slow pace if you just push the left joystick forward. Press it in, and they’ll break into a light jog that doesn’t use any stamina. Press it again or hold the left stick, and they’ll go into a full run that burns stamina, but also counts as cardio. Trying to swap between a jog and a run can wind up feeling a little clumsy if you hate pressing a stick as a button.

You can change that by going into Settings, tabbing over to Gameplay, and scrolling down to Movement. Here, you’ll find three settings that will help control how fast you move. The most important one is Movement Speed. This changes what max speed you reach when moving the joystick. It’s set to walk by default, but you can change that to Fast Walk, Jog, or Run. Note that Run doesn’t change default to your fastest possible speed, but rather your top speed before you’ll start burning stamina. Don’t be afraid to experiment in that menu and find the default speed that feels most natural to you.

You can also change your Combat Movement Speed separately, which determines how you’ll move in a shootout. By default, it’s set to Fast Walk, but you can similarly set it to Walk, Jog, and Run as well.

If you want to speed things along just a little more, you can also toggle Stand & Sprint on. When crouching in GTA 6, clicking the left stick will make you hustle forward a little faster in that crouched state. This option will instead snap you into a standing position out of a crouch when you run. So if stealth isn’t really your style, this will make sure you can get the jump on enemies faster.

There are plenty more handy options to check out in GTA 6’s Settings menu, including a host of accessibility features that will let you change minigame controls, button holding prompts, and more. Make sure to poke around and fine tune the game to your liking if anything feels off.
